#5852. Heliene and Caelux combine PV cells and solar glass for a hybrid module

Heliene, a solar modules manufacturer, and Caelux Corporation, a perovskite solar technology company, are starting commercial production of their Hybrid-Tandem solar module.

This module combines perovskite glass from Caelux and silicon N-type cells from Heliene, placing two energy generating sources in a single solar panel. Heliene is producing the modules in its plant in Mountain Iron, Minnesota, with first deliveries slated for 2027.

“One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” said Martin Pochtaruk, CEO and founder of Heliene. “With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar, besides the fact that partnering with true friends also makes it fun.”

The companies are reporting a 27% efficiency from the Hybrid-Tandem module. Heliene and Caelux desiged this module to have a higher power density in a smaller project footprint.

“Heliene is a true leader in U.S. manufacturing, and we share a belief that when we lead the market, our customers win. Together, we’re commercializing ultra-high-efficiency solar modules that will set a new bar for American-made solar,” said Caelux CEO Scott Graybeal.

Heliene will showcase the Hybrid-Tandem module at RE+ in Las Vegas from Nov. 17 to 19, at booth #W16546.

#5850. Trump Administration Continues Systematic Dismantling of Public Lands

Proposed Rule Would Shut the Public Out and Allow the Administration to Make Sweeping Decisions About 250 Million Acres of Western Public Lands Behind Closed Doors

Yesterday, the Administration announced a proposed Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rulemaking that would drastically weaken the public’s involvement in land use planning and gut protections for Areas of Critical Environmental Concern (ACECs), one of BLM’s primary conservation designations, across 245 million acres of Western public lands. The rule proposes to stifle the voices of local communities by significantly shortening public comment periods and cutting out robust environmental analysis. These changes would make it easier for the BLM to fast-track the sale, transfer, or use of public lands for oil and gas drilling, mining, data centers, and other industrial or commercial development, all while shutting out the American people. The announcement kicks off a 60 day comment period (January 9th deadline).

The public lands overseen by the BLM contain crucial wildlife corridors, critical habitat, cultural resources and landscapes, watersheds, historic sites, and access to nature and scenery.  The rule threatens to strip vital safeguards for ACECs and environmental review that protect these values, leaving the West’s most sensitive lands vulnerable to irreparable harm.

This aggressive regulatory rollback is the latest chapter in a coordinated, systematic dismantling of America’s public lands. It directly connects to a broader pattern of hostility toward balanced stewardship, which includes the recent rescission of the landmark Public Lands Rule, stated intention to roll back the Roadless Rule and Wilderness policies, the evisceration of National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) standards, and repeated attempts to give away public lands to corporations and developers. This rulemaking contributes to this administration’s singular focus: fast-tracking industrial exploitation and drilling at the expense of our shared heritage, tribal sovereignty and the outdoor recreation economies that sustain rural Western communities.

The proposal comes as Congress debates permitting legislation that would also weaken public participation in decisions affecting shared lands and give more power to development interests.

Planning serves as the foundational blueprints governing public lands for decades; eroding these processes is a profound threat to the long-term health of the West. Making robust environmental review optional and weakening ACEC standards intentionally ties the agency’s hands, preventing it from effectively responding to the compounding threats of climate change, drought, and habitat fragmentation. This action rejects the unmistakable demand from the American public, including local leaders, Tribal representatives, and local elected officials, who have consistently called for public lands to be managed transparently and protected for future generations.

“The Trump Administration is once again plotting to undermine our world-renowned system of shared lands and the public processes that guide their management,” said Jackie Feinberg, Sierra Club’s National Lands Conservation Manager. “Weakening protections and public participation would fast-track the industrialization and privatization of places essential for wildlife, clean water, cultural and historic preservation, and access to nature. We stand firmly against these attempts to cut out the “public” from public lands for the benefit of corporate polluters and profiteers.”

“Gutting transparency, review, and public engagement requirements within the West’s most ecologically sensitive wildlife corridors, watersheds, and cultural resources are the actions of cowards trying to fast-track industrial development at any and all social costs,” said Kara Matsumoto, senior policy director at the Conservation Lands Foundation. “Resource management plans are the blueprints for keeping public lands and waters healthy, and weakening them will weaken local economies and fragile ecosystems. We’ll continue to fight this corporate greed because the overwhelming majority of Americans want more nature protected, not less.”

“The opportunity to review and comment on land management actions keeps the public in public lands.” said Hilary Eisen, federal policy director at Wild Montana. “Resource management plans provide the long-term framework for how vast swaths of public land across the West are managed and it is essential that these plans be crafted with robust public engagement. This proposed rule sidelines the public, as well as local, state, and tribal governments, in BLM land use planning.”

“Resource management planning is meant to provide the public a real say in how BLM manages our shared public lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern are how the agency turns that input into on-the-ground protections for special places and important wildlife habitat,” said Maddy Munson, senior policy and planning specialist at Defenders of Wildlife. “Cutting back public participation and narrowing the agency’s analysis isn’t streamlining, but rather stacking the deck against the places and species that need protection the most.”

“For Nevadans public land is our way of life. Whether we have jobs dependent on mining, grazing, the outdoor industry or just love taking our families camping, these public lands in Nevada are a huge part of who we are. We want to have an active role in determining how these lands are managed and efforts to take the public out of this planning process and weaken protections are just wrong,” said Shaaron Netherton, Executive Director at Friends of Nevada WIlderness. “We need to stand up and keep the public in our public lands.”

“The Trump administration continues to eliminate tools that the Bureau of Land Management has relied on for decades for conserving wildlife habitat, protecting clean water, and working with local communities. The objective is clear: replace the multiple uses and values of our public lands with the singular use of fossil fuel development. That agenda has no footing in Colorado, where 96% percent of Coloradans support conserving public lands and open space and 81% believe oil and gas development is not an acceptable use of public lands,” said Juli Slivka, Senior Director of Policy and Programs at Wilderness Workshop.

“These are the plans that decide whether a valley gets drilled or a trout stream gets protected, and this proposal is built to make those decisions faster and with fewer people in the room,” said Bobby McEnaney, Senior Lands Analyst at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council). “Cutting the public’s time to weigh in by two thirds, scrapping the full environmental review, and letting a political appointee invoke an emergency to skip the rest is not modernization. It is a way to lock in drilling and mining decisions before anyone can object. Governors get 30 days and no appeal, Tribal plans drop out of the review entirely, and the agency gives itself the power to shrink or erase existing protected areas. Interior should withdraw this proposal and keep the public’s seat at the table.”

“These lands are called “public lands” for a reason: They are owned by the people of the United States. The Bureau of Land Management’s job is to manage them in the public’s interest, for the common good. By so severely restricting opportunities for the public—including, importantly, Tribal Nations—to be involved in planning for their management, the BLM is depriving all of us of our rights as the owners,” said Michael Painter, Coordinator, Californians for Western Wilderness.

“The Trump administration continues its relentless agenda of handing over public lands to corporations,” said Thomas Delehanty, senior attorney with Earthjustice’s Rocky Mountain Office. “Cutting the public out of land management benefits no one except the extractive industries hellbent on controlling these shared resources for their own private gain. Anyone who values public lands must be loud and clear: these attacks end now.”

“Public lands belong to all Americans, and decisions about their future should be made through transparent processes informed by science, meaningful public participation and consultation with Tribes and others in the community. This proposed rule would give us less of a say in the management of 245 million acres of our shared lands and weaken areas of critical environmental concern, the BLM’s primary tool for protecting important natural and cultural sites. It is another clear attempt to give drilling, mining and other development interests more influence over our public lands, in the same spirit as rescission of the BLM Public Lands Rule—and only days after voters delivered a stinging rebuke to this administration’s agenda of doing favors for oil and gas companies and other powerful corporations. Our public lands deserve better, and so do future generations that will inherit them.” said Michael Carroll, BLM Campaign Director, The Wilderness Society.

“In New Mexico, the BLM planning process gives communities, Pueblos, Tribes, acequias, recreationalists, conservation organizations, ranchers, hunters and anglers a real say in what happens to the 13.5 million acres of public land that the agency manages here,” said Sally Paez, senior staff attorney for New Mexico Wild. “Places like the Greater Chaco landscape, the Permian Basin’s remaining wildlife habitat, and our desert grasslands have protections today because New Mexicans showed up and spoke out during planning. New Mexicans shouldn’t be shut out of decisions about their own public lands.”

“In Oregon, the BLM manages 2.6 million acres of Oregon and California Lands that are home to imperiled wildlife, endemic botanical resources, wild rivers, and climate change-mitigating ancient forests that provide outstanding recreational opportunities and socioeconomic benefits to Oregonians and all Americans,” said Susan Jane Brown, attorney with Silvix Resources. “The public and other stakeholders must have a central role in the science-informed stewardship of these cherished resources, all of which will be placed at risk of existential loss with BLM’s proposed rulemaking.”

“Oregon’s high desert community has modeled a long, successful history of federal planners, tribal interests, ranchers, hunters and anglers, recreationists, and conservationists working together to craft management strategies that balance land use and promote conservation across 12 million acres of our shared public lands,” said Mark Salvo, Senior Conservation Advisor for Oregon Natural Desert Association. “Now the Trump administration is recklessly dismissing these decades of collaboration and compromise, trampling public processes, and sidelining those who have worked to protect these lands and resources for future generations–all to advance a narrow agenda of exploitation at the expense of the public interest.”

“The public lands are the people’s lands and the American people have spoken loud and clear. The Bureau’s proposal to cut public participation, reduce protections for cultural sites and critically important habitat, and shortcut environmental analysis is just one more indication that the Trump Administration isn’t listening and will do anything to silence the public, Tribes, and scientists and ignore the reality of what’s happening on the ground,” said Josh Osher, public policy director for Western Watersheds Project. “Millions of acres of climate-stressed Bureau-managed lands are already being degraded by extractive industries, and we need planning rules that include thorough and honest science-based assessments and as many voices as possible to help improve ecological conditions and resilience.”

This is just the latest attempt from the Trump Administration to dismantle our public lands piece by piece,” said Sandra Schubert, Executive Director of Tuleyome. “The proposed Planning Rule undermines protections that ensure that our public lands and wild forests remain accessible and are used sustainably. Resource management plans are built on science and centuries of management experience. They give local land managers and communities the ability to maintain healthy ecosystems while supporting the diverse ways communities depend on public lands. Undermining planning undermines our public lands”

“Once again, Doug Burgum is doing everything in his power to cut the public out of public lands,” said Aaron Weiss, executive director of the Center for Western Priorities. “This new rule gives political appointees in DC more power to shrink protected places and ignore local voices. Public lands belong to all of us, and good land use planning means giving everyone the chance to weigh in.”

“America’s national parks are supported by the public lands that surround them, and this proposal is another blatant attempt to unravel decades of conservation progress that the public overwhelmingly supports,” said Beau Kiklis, associate director of energy and landscape conservation at the National Parks Conservation Association. “Roughly 80 national park sites share a border with BLM lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern have helped protect Dinosaur National Monument from impacts of oil and gas development, support Joshua Tree’s wildlife by protecting the neighboring Pinto Mountains, and protect ancestral sites near Hovenweep among countless others. This is another attempt to sell off and sell out our public lands, and the public deserves a real say before more is lost.”

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. For more information, visit www.sierraclub.org.

#5842. California orders utilities to develop joint DER orchestration framework

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The October order also directed PG&E, SCE and SDG&E to “more explicitly” consider flexible demand, a move one regulator said could reduce interconnection delays.

The order aims to harness DERs to meet local electricity needs, support grid reliability, reduce or defer infrastructure upgrades, and advance California’s electrification and decarbonization goals, the CPUC said.

“Our decision moves the state toward a common framework for the utilities to manage and forecast DERs on our system, and create visibility for the California Independent System Operator,” CPUC Commissioner Darcie Houck said in a statement.

The order gives Pacific Gas & Electric, Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric one year to develop a joint DER orchestration proposal that meets dozens of CPUC requirements, including “open and interoperable” communication; data sharing; cybersecurity; ratepayer protections; clear customer participation pathways; recognizing locational and temporal value; and avoiding double compensation for DER owners.

The framework will be developed in a working group process that considers input from stakeholders representing ratepayers, energy service providers, community choice aggregators and others. The process will establish “a common set of rules and policies across California” that the utilities would implement over time based on technological readiness, the CPUC said.

The working group must consider a range of technical, market and customer-facing issues related to DER orchestration, including methodologies for assessing cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit balance; DERs’ visibility to distribution system operators; DER aggregators’ role; technology ownership; flexible dispatch; “fair and non-discriminatory participation” for both utility and non-utility DER providers; and performance measurement, monitoring and accountability, according to the CPUC’s order.

Separately, the CPUC ordered utilities to evaluate how flexible electric loads can mitigate grid constraints and advance electrification as DERs become more common on California’s grid. Like standardized DER orchestration, planning scenarios that contemplate load flexibility may also help reduce burdens on ratepayers, the commission said.

Planning scenarios that “more explicitly” account for flexible demand will complement existing demand planning scenarios and focus on how dynamic changes in electric load — from shifting electric vehicle charging times or charging and discharging stationary batteries — could affect the timing, size and need for grid upgrades, the CPUC said.

In a statement, CPUC Commissioner Christine Harada said the order would help California utilities make “better use of the grid we already have,” reduce interconnection delays and avoid costly system upgrades. It would also make it easier for homes and businesses to electrify, she said.

“Our decision gives families and businesses more options to charge a car, electrify a home, or expand operations while reducing the need for costly upgrades. Those options need to be easy to understand and easy to use, people shouldn’t need an engineering degree to benefit,” Harada said.

#5837. No home left behind: Scaling VPP participation while maintaining customer control

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Utilities that redesign demand management programs around how customers actually behave will be the ones to boost participation and system flexibility, writes Uplight’s Gisela Glandt.

Gisela Glandt is vice president of virtual power plants at Uplight, a provider of utility demand management solutions.

Load growth is back, and it isn't slowing down. Electrification, data centers and extreme weather are pushing utilities to find flexible capacity faster than they can build it. Demand-side programs including demand response, virtual power plants, time-varying rates and energy efficiency are one of the few levers that scale quickly and cost-effectively — yet the industry keeps hitting the same wall.

Roughly 80% of customers say they want help managing their energy, but utilities are still seeing enrollment in demand management programs around 10% — despite larger incentives, more innovative technology, and more targeted marketing. What if the problem isn't the customers and instead is the process of asking them to raise their hand?

Opt-in utility program enrollment puts the burden on the customer: to understand the program, check to see if they are eligible, decide it's worth it, and then take action. The benefits and incentives can show up months down the road, and they may even forget about them. Most people don’t make it past enrollment and it’s not because of lack of interest. It simply involves too many steps and too much brain power.

The industry is shifting from programs customers must join to flexibility that's already embedded as a default or activated at the point of sale of a device, with no enrollment required. Where utilities have made this shift, customer participation climbs from 10% into the 70% to 100% range. One Midwestern utility that restructured a program from opt-in to opt-out scaled capacity four to five times faster — and had 70% to 80% of customers participate.

“Opt-out" can be translated as "no choice,” and that couldn’t be further from the truth. A well-designed built-in flexibility program ensures that the customer stays in control. Instead of asking everyone to opt in to participate, it lets anyone choose not to participate at any time, with control that's visible, immediate, and intuitively easy. However, default programs only work when customers are really in control.

Behavioral demand response programs cast the broadest net with no hardware required, no cost of entry, and are open to nearly every energy customer. That's what makes it the most equitable and accessible path in: it reaches the renters and non-device-owners that automated demand response leaves out.

Device manufacturer-based programs work the other angle, unlocking capacity that's already installed and sitting idle: smart thermostats, connected water heaters, electric vehicles and batteries not yet enrolled in anything. When enrollment happens by default at device setup — through OEM partnerships rather than a separate utility sign-up — that latent capacity becomes dispatchable. The shifts are smaller and steadier than a typical demand response event, but can have even greater impact as participation scales exponentially.

For both types of programs, customers have the option to participate and receive benefits, and there are no consequences if they opt out of a particular event or day.

Participation in demand-management programs is an affordability strategy. Every home added to a utility’s flexible base expands the pool of dispatchable megawatts — and the more flexibility utilities can call on, the more generation they can defer or avoid. Deferred capital is downward pressure on rates. With affordability under scrutiny from regulators and customers alike, participation stops being a program metric and becomes an affordability lever.

A low-friction entry program can be an on-ramp for higher value programs. Customers who join a behavioral or OEM-based demand response program are now more informed and better targets for automated demand response, time-varying rates, managed EV charging, energy efficiency and other programs.

The utilities that redesign enrollment around how customers actually behave, with effortless enrollment and complete customer control, will be the ones that close the participation gap. Reliability and affordability increasingly depend on getting this right, with energy customers seeing the most immediate benefits.

#5835. Science For The People, Right On!

Today United for the Future launches at COP31 today with a plan to unite 100 million people in peaceful, non-partisan marches in cities worldwide. Their goal is to assemble the largest coordinated climate demonstration in history in order to put climate action back at the top of the political agenda.

Backers of the initiative include Christiana Figueres, former UN climate chief and a key architect of the Paris Agreement; Bill McKibben, author and co-founder of 350.org; Ram Ramanathan of Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego; and Sandrine Dixson-Declève, honorary president of the Club of Rome.

Together, they beckon citizens around the world: “Protect our future. Act on the science.” Their call asks governments to stop weakening climate protections and to deliver action that cuts emissions and protects nature in line with science.

Limiting temperature rise to a 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it’s been a focus of international climate negotiations, and one that’s often been politically contentious.

“For too many people, climate change is deadly,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell said at COP31. “At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock. Rewire the global economy for the electric age. Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms, and governments.”

Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026, driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict, according to new research by the Global Carbon Project.

Then there’s the recent blue tsunami that took place in the US midterm elections, which served as a condemnation of the Trump administration. Historian and activist Rebecca Solnit exclaims, “It was a dam breaking, the dam that held back the will of the people, the people of the world’s most diverse country, the people who believed in their own rights and equality and in the rights and equality of others.”

Now, through promised agendas to increase affordability for consumers, Democrats have a keen opportunity to foreground science as a way to accomplish goals. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) admonishes the new Democratic majority to deliver on its campaign jargon. “No more empty rhetoric. No more telling us how terrible Trump and the Republicans are. No more excuses,” he says. “We now have the votes to pass legislation that will demonstrably improve the lives of millions of working families. And that’s what we must do.”

Sanders insists that the time is now to “act boldly.” Democrats can create millions of good-paying jobs, he continues, “by moving our energy systems away from fossil fuels to energy efficiency and sustainable energy.”

David Fickling outlines in Bloomberg this week that renewables have already made tremendous headway, to the point that “sometimes, change comes at you so fast that you forget to congratulate yourself on what you’ve achieved.”

In 2025 clean energy sources generated nearly the same amount of electricity as the entire world consumed in 1996. About half of that electricity, Fickling continues, was sourced from wind and solar power.

“Instead of concentrating on squeezing the final tons of carbon from electricity,” he offers, “governments need to make abundant clean power cheap enough to drive fossil fuels out of everything else — in particular, electric cars and trucks, home heating systems, and the sort of low-temperature heat used in food and paper manufacturing.”

In that new cohort of leaders is William Lawrence, co-founder of the climate action movement, Sunrise. The Michigan Democrat flipped a House seat and sees clean energy as a way to fulfill campaign promises.

He describes clean energy tax credits as a good place to start.

“It’s a huge issue not just for the climate, but for our energy security,” he states. Climate is as important to energy security as it’s ever been, he tells Claire Brown of the New York Times.” People are experiencing the rising costs of fuel due to the war and volatility around the world. And we can all see the value of being able to have cheap, clean renewable energy that doesn’t depend on the global commodity markets.”

Several scientists and physicians were elected to the US Congress as part of the reinvigoration of science at the federal level. “The importance of having scientists, engineers, and health professionals in national, state, and local political positions cannot be overstated,” relates Deborah D. Stine, the executive director of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology during the Obama administration. “If the policy question is outside their own expertise, they know how to call on the best experts.”

The incoming scientists represent “a real repudiation of what has been two terrible years for science and public health,” Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, chronicles for Alexander Nazaryan of the New York Times.

Where will the US Congress go from here? Rebecca Solnit muses, “What comes after hope, when hope is realized, when hope is no longer necessary?”

Clean energy expert Steve Hanley has an answer to that question. “The guiding star for all policy decisions going forward should be reducing carbon and methane emissions.”

Did you know that electric motors convert 90% of the energy they consume into motion, while an internal combustion engine converts less than 30%? Not everyone is aware of the efficiency of electrifying everything, though. Some scientists are already talking about the important need to draw in a new generation of clean energy advocates among Republicans in Congress and everyday life.

“In almost all circumstances, electrification is a good thing,” says Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister of climate change and energy and COP31’s president of negotiations.

Now we’ll see if Congress can translate political subterfuge into clean energy reality.

Carolyn Fortuna, PhD, is a longtime journalist and researcher for CleanTechnica who frequently writes about climate science, renewable energy, and environmental communication. #5832. The Netherlands Has €231 Million for Cleaner Inland Ships. It Still Needs Electric Freight Corridors.

The Netherlands is preparing to spend €231.2 million over four years helping inland ships replace fossil-fuel propulsion. The first €36.93 million tender opens on November 17, 2026, and battery-electric vessels are among the eligible investments. This is a serious step toward decarbonizing freight on the waterways that link Dutch ports and Europe's industrial heartland. But the programme's most important scoring calculation rewards emissions avoided per euro of propulsion subsidy while excluding separate subsidies for the shore infrastructure on which the ship may depend. That distinction matters when the commercial product is a complete freight service, not an electric vessel sitting beside a quay.

The new Dutch tender is considerably more sophisticated than a technology demonstration fund, yet it leaves an important accounting boundary. My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment follows that boundary from subsidized vessels to working routes, drawing on my open, 98-page Inland Freight Electrification report.

The RVO programme can support battery-electric systems, some hybrid arrangements and other propulsion technologies, together with eligible charging and refueling facilities. Its published explanation prioritizes electrification where practical. That is sensible: electric inland vessels are already operating in the Netherlands, and a subsidy should encourage the pathway that provides the required service at low emissions and acceptable cost.

The scheme also recognizes that a vessel does not operate in isolation. Applications receive points for commercial cooperation, cargo-owner agreements and the quality of supporting infrastructure arrangements. These are material criteria, not decorative promises. They are a welcome correction to programmes that fund novel equipment and assume the market, terminal and utility will somehow arrange everything else.

Yet most of the available points are tied to projected emissions reductions per euro of propulsion support. That is a consistent measure for comparing applications for individual ships. It is not an accounting of the entire investment required to turn a diesel freight route into an electric one. One barge may need access to battery exchange at both ends of its journey, reserve battery inventory, grid capacity, a crane or handling system and a dependable service agreement. Some of those facilities can serve many vessels, making it hard to allocate their cost and value to any single propulsion application.

Zero Emission Services, or ZES, has already shown what putting the pieces together looks like. Its swappable battery containers allow inland vessels to obtain charged energy without each owner purchasing and maintaining every battery required by the route. At Moerdijk, a terminal arrangement combines battery exchange, handling equipment and access to an existing electricity connection. The ZES network is extending beyond isolated demonstrations, although operating sites, planned stations and funded vessel conversions must not be counted as the same thing.

The difference between a capable ship and reliable freight is familiar to ports. Charged batteries must be available at the right time, terminals must handle exchanges without disrupting cargo work, and the energy-service provider needs enough committed traffic to finance its containers and chargers.

The Netherlands deserves credit for recognizing these dependencies. It need not discard vessel-level grants or wait until every future route is planned before making early awards. But a second programme-level measure is needed alongside emissions per propulsion subsidy: what complete, repeatable electric freight service is each funded project helping create, and which shared assets make that service possible?

This matters all the more because the freight being carried will change. Fossil-linked cargo is likely to decline as coal and petroleum use falls, and ports should not size batteries, terminals and connections around the assumption that today's bulk flows continue indefinitely. A route with strong contracted demand may justify shared charging equipment while a low-utilization route requires a different architecture or timetable. The answer depends on the freight task, not merely on the specifications of an available vessel.

The Dutch programme is a promising way to accelerate the first investments. Its next achievement should be to show that those investments connect: cargo moving on named routes, vessels using dependable shared energy infrastructure, and operating data strong enough to finance the following corridor without perpetually reinventing the subsidy. The ship is the visible part of the transition. The corridor is what makes it commercially useful.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines the subsidy rules, the Moerdijk battery-exchange arrangement and the difference between vessel awards and operational corridors. The open, 98-page Inland Freight Electrification report contains the modelled cargo, fleet, battery-pool, terminal and investment evidence behind that analysis.

#5831. Constellation pursues hybrid capacity contracts alongside nuclear uprates

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The offering gives Constellation “a new way to pair the existing fleet with incremental capacity” by adding batteries, generation and demand response, CEO Joe Dominguez said.

Constellation Energy is pursuing a new kind of bilateral contract with large customers that combines clean baseload power generation — likely nuclear — with other capacity resources such as battery storage, demand response and new generation, executives said this week.

The company is calling the offering “Peak+” and bills it as a simpler, cheaper and more environmentally friendly alternative to new gas-fired generation for hyperscalers and other large power consumers.

“Peak+ is going to be broadly defined as bringing capacity solutions plus existing clean and reliable generation,” Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s chairman, president and CEO, said on a Monday quarterly earnings call with investors and stock analysts.

Constellation is introducing the hybrid contracts as construction delays, cost overruns, interconnection delays and long-term fuel-price uncertainty present material risks for power plant developers, he said. He also pointed to the “political tilt in this last election,” which he said raises the specter of stronger federal regulation on carbon emissions affecting fossil fuel-powered plants.

“Constellation Peak+ gives us a new way to pair the existing fleet with incremental capacity,” he said. “We could add batteries and generation supply at our plants given the vast amount of land that we own around the plants.”

A slide in Constellation’s third-quarter investor presentation showed Peak+ pricing $20/MWh to $50/MWh higher than the “floor” set by the federal production tax credit for nuclear power but lower than the $110/MWh to $130/MWh levelized cost of power from new-build combined-cycle gas turbines in the PJM Interconnection’s eastern region — where much of Constellation’s nuclear capacity sits — by 2032, assuming a $3,000/kW build cost.

The production tax credit pays nuclear generating units up to $15/MWh when revenues fall between $26/MWh and $44.75/MWh, Constellation says.

The company signed its first Peak+ customer for a 20-year agreement for 270 MW of “unit-contingent energy, capacity and attributes from our existing nuclear fleet,” according to a press release. Dominguez declined to identify the customer.

He said he still expects some customers will pursue new large power plants or off-grid solutions. However, pairing “simpler and less risky capacity solutions with our large volume of clean energy is a compelling solution,” he said.

At about 55 GW, the Baltimore-based independent power producer says it has the largest combined fleet of nuclear, natural gas and geothermal generation in the U.S.

About 22 GW of that is nuclear, much of it in the capacity-constrained PJM Interconnection.

The company has announced more than 1 GW of hyperscaler-backed capacity expansions at existing nuclear power plants in recent weeks, including an 890-MW agreement with Google and a 190-MW deal with Amazon.

“I know that there's been some chatter that once we sold the [nuclear power] uprates, our ability to contract the existing fleet would somehow be exhausted — it is not,” Dominguez said.

In addition to the new Peak+ contracts, the company has “not finished exploring uprates at plants,” he said.

Dominguez also said the company’s planned nuclear restart at the site formerly known as Three Mile Island — now renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center — is on track for the second half of 2027 with the first fuel assemblies and transformers are on site.

Separately, Constellation announced another addition to its non-nuclear generating fleet, which grew dramatically in the past year following its $16.4 billion combination with gas-heavy Calpine.

Constellation said in September that it would pay Shell Energy North America $715 million to buy the Rhode Island State Energy Center, a 609-MW combined-cycle gas-fired power plant in the ISO New England wholesale market. RISEC will run on a merchant basis, Constellation said.

#5829. Roll-A-Rack debuting low-profile, manufactured-on-site solar racking

Roll-A-Rack, a developer of patented, on-site-manufactured solar racking systems, will introduce SunChord, its new multi-purpose ground-mounted system, at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.

SunChord is a low-profile solar racking designed to use less land than conventional fixed-tilt racking or trackers. It is composed of two components: gutter channels and clamp brackets that attach to solar panels. SunChord assembles using what Roll-A-Rack has dubbed its “snap-slide-secure” system.

“The next generation of solar technology needs to do more than produce clean electricity. It needs to make better use of land, minimize environmental impacts and create value beyond the energy generated,” said Don Scipione, founder of Roll-A-Rack. “SunChord reflects our vision of harmonizing sun and earth, combining solar energy production with rainwater harvesting and soil conservation in a system that can unlock new opportunities for solar development on land where conventional approaches fall short.”

Roll-A-Rack claims an array using SunChord can capture 95% of rain that falls it using its racking channels to redirect the water. The company sees potential for the racking in agrivoltaic applications, sites with land constraints, on brownfields and where ground disturbance should be limited.

SunChord is assembled on-site using a roll-forming device similar to producing roof-edge gutters. SunChord was developed with support from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Integrated Energy Systems Office and the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture. The company has two issued U.S. patents, a patent application pending, wind-tunnel ratings and UL 2703 certification.

Roll-A-Rack is planning to supply SunChord for up to five pilot projects. Interested EPCs and developers can contact the company at [email protected].

#5826. Data centers could lower your electricity bill. Will utilities let them?

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

When sales increase more than costs, rates should decline. But some utilities are using lower historical sales data with updated cost assumptions to “lock in” higher rates, writes Edward Burgess.

Edward Burgess is a partner at Current Energy Group.

The debate over the impacts of new data centers on customers' electricity bills is only intensifying.

On the one hand, many people blame data center companies for triggering new grid costs that others will pay. On the other, data centers hold great promise to lower customer bills.

For the latter, the theory is that, as high-utilization infrastructure users, data centers can absorb a large share of fixed costs that would otherwise be charged to existing customers.

To their credit, nearly 200 data center companies have signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to pay their fair share of costs. However, achieving this commitment depends on cooperative action by local utilities to update their rates accordingly.

This raises an important question: Are investor-owned utilities willing to share the benefits of large-load growth with existing customers? Recent evidence suggests otherwise in some cases.

To fully understand this problem, let’s revisit the fundamentals of electricity ratemaking.

New rates are typically proposed by utilities but ultimately approved by state utility regulators. When utilities propose new rates, the core calculation is based on two key inputs: 1) utility costs in the numerator, and 2) utility sales in the denominator.

If the denominator increases more than the numerator (i.e., sales increase more than costs), then customer rates should decline on average.

But in the era of hyperscale load growth, the specifics of these inputs — how they are defined and when relative changes occur — matter a great deal. In several recent cases, utilities have simply neglected to increase kWh sales from new data center load in their rate proposals, while still including related cost increases.

For example, in North Carolina, Duke Energy recently proposed increasing customer rates by over 15% over the next two years.

However, this increase was based on a rate calculation that kept the denominator essentially frozen at 2024 levels — even though Duke had already contracted to add hundreds of MWs of new data centers in the coming years, and included costs triggered by this in its proposal.

Current Energy Group analyzed Duke’s proposal and presented expert testimony to the North Carolina Utilities Commission on behalf of the state’s Attorney General’s office. We found that 54% of the requested rate increase — approximately $1 billion annually — could be erased if kWh sales in the rate formula were simply corrected to reflect Duke’s own planning assumptions.

In fact, correcting just the kWh sales figure and one other key variable — return on equity — was enough to turn the proposed 15% rate increase into a 4% decrease, even with significant new grid investments.

A similar pattern emerged in Missouri, where Evergy Missouri Metro included costs for new gas generation to serve new data centers but did not account for the increased sales to those data centers in its rate calculation. As data center sales ramp up, the utility would see a windfall over the four years the new rates are in effect.

In Louisiana, increased sales from a new Meta data center could trigger an immediate customer refund over the next three years. Instead, Entergy proposed accounting methods to defer that benefit over a 20-year period.

This “one simple trick” of immediately updating kWh sales in the rate formula could save customers billions in the coming years. So why do utility rate proposals keep failing to account for data center load growth?

Some utility analysts might point to arcane explanations, such as the traditional practice of using a “historic test year.” There may be a grain of truth to that, but it is not a convincing argument given widespread concerns about affordability.

Duke, for instance, had the legal ability to propose a forward-looking Multi-Year Rate Plan but chose not to include any load growth in its rate proposal.

A more cynical view is that utilities are seeking to “lock in” higher rates before new data center load fully materializes and the denominator rises. This creates a major windfall for utilities, at least temporarily, as data center load ramps up before rates can catch up.

Traditionally, utilities have complained about “regulatory lag,” which arises when rates are not increased quickly enough to capture rising costs. Now, in the era of hyperscale load growth, we have the opposite problem — a “reverse regulatory lag.” Instead, rates are not being reduced quickly enough to capture rising revenue from large loads.

This problem is exacerbated by another challenge: As utilities slow-walk updates to the denominator (kWh sales), they speed-run updates to the numerator (costs recovered).

Many utilities, including Duke, use accelerated cost recovery mechanisms, such as Construction Work in Progress, to fund new infrastructure for load growth.

This further strains affordability. Infrastructure costs are front-loaded through near-term rate increases, while any rate relief from load growth won’t materialize for years.

Under Duke’s original proposal, customers would pay for the construction of new gas-fired power plants four years before they start operating, and six years before data center load appears in the denominator.

As affordability concerns persist, what solutions should regulators consider?

Whether hyperscale load growth raises or lowers bills depends on how and when the numerator and denominator are updated. Understanding these mechanics and the options for mitigating them will shape how regulators and stakeholders weigh the bill impacts of large load growth.

#5824. The Perovskite Solar Cell Kraken Has Been Unleashed Upon The US

Perovskite is a relatively inexpensive material that has attracted thousands of researchers since 2009, when a team of scientists in Japan first demonstrated its use in solar cells. They achieved a solar energy conversion efficiency of little more than 3%, but since science loves a challenge, that was just the beginning of the story. In the latest chapter, the US firms Heliene and Caeulux have just introduced a new perovskite-enabled solar module that hits the jackpot at up to 27% efficiency, and it is already in commercial production, no less.

So far in the renewable energy transition, silicon has shouldered much of the heavy lifting due to its excellent solar conversion properties. Still, silicon is relatively expensive material that demands a complex manufacturing process. Perovskite is the reverse. Based on a naturally occurring mineral, synthetic perovskites can be lab-grown and applied to solar cell fabrication in a high volume, high throughput process similar to roll-to-roll manufacturing and other solution-based methods (see lots more perovskite background here).

There being no such thing as a free lunch, “raw” perovskite is challenged by natural conditions, namely, humidity. Tweaking the formula with other, more durable materials can resolve that problem. Researchers have also developed a tandem solution, in which a perovskite layer rests upon a silicon layer, providing an efficiency boost while minimizing the additional cost.

In the US solar market, the sticky wicket is the current state of federal energy, trade, and tax polices. Still, the red-hot demand for solar energy in the US has motivated solar stakeholders to steamroll over those obstacles, attracting overseas investors (here’s one example) as well as new domestic ventures.

On the domestic side, the Corning-backed manufacturer Heliene has been focusing on silicon while the startup Caelux has tackled the perovskite solar cell challenge with a glass substrate that can be layered onto other materials in a solar module. Now the two manufacturers have combined forces, with Caelux’s perovskite-doped glass boosting the conversion efficiency of Heliene’s N-type solar cells by up to 20%.

The Caelux-Heliene mashup comes at a time when Congress has finally put the wheels in motion to streamline the permitting process for energy projects. The two firms already have a running head start. On November 10, the two firms announced that commercial-scale production has already begun on their Hybrid-Tandem™ solar module

“Manufactured by Heliene in Minnesota, the perovskite plus silicon technology combines Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass with Heliene’s established silicon module platform to construct a solar module with two separate power generation layers that deliver higher power density,” Heliene explains.

“One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” added Martin Pochtaruk, Heliene CEO and Founder, in a press statement.

“With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar,” Pochtaruk emphasized.

Stay tuned for the next development. The new modules are now in production at Heliene’s manufacturing facility Minnesota, with deliveries set for 2027. That’s just for starters. Caelux and Heliene have already targeted 29% efficiency and up for their next-generation modules.

The conversion efficiency improvement is the gift that keeps on giving. In the rooftop solar sector, for example, high-efficiency solar cells enable developers to squeeze more electricity out of a given space, making a rooftop array more economical for smaller properties that are otherwise shut out of the market. The cost of a smaller, more effcient array can also ripple downwards in the form of savings on labor, hardware, and transportation expenses.

For rooftop solar in general, the boost in efficiency provides an opportunity to take full advantage of power sharing programs with local utilities, which enable solar owners to earn revenue and qualify for time-of-use discounts. The benefits can ripple into home energy storage systems and home EV charging as well.

On a larger scale, the space-saving angle can help alleviate land use conflicts that otherwise stymie solar development, particularly in the area of farm-to-solar conversion.

Although real estate development is by far the primary factor driving the loss of farmland in the US, solar opponents (looking at you, Brooke Rollins) have played the farm card to gin up resistance to solar development in rural communities. With efficiency improvements, the economic case improves for solar arrays on marginal lands and smaller parcels. That can be partcularly helpful in the community solar field, where solar arrays are typically smaller.

Additionally, the improved efficiency can help accelerate the uptake of agrivoltaic practices that balance energy-producing solar panels with grazing and croplands. These dual-use arrays can enable farmers to continue working their land while guaranteeing a revenue stream from the solar developer.

Furthermore, high-efficiency solar opens up new opportunities in the field of floating solar, where developers can make use of reservoirs and other human-engineered bodies of water instead of taking up space on land. By taking up less room on water for the same power generation capacity, floating solar can also squeeze into reservoirs where recreation and habitat conservation also compete for space.

Perovskite solar cells represent just one key breakthrough area in the US solar industry. Easing the federal energy permitting bottleneck is another. That can be a two-edged sword, enabling more fossil energy resources to flow through the pipeline. However, permitting reform could also prevent the fossil energy industry from running amok through federal energy policy.

Members of Congress are currently negotiating over the particulars of Senate Bill 5653, aka the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. If enacted as envisioned by the solar industry, the reforms will put a crimp in Trump’s “American Energy Dominance” policy, which has placed new and burdensome restrictions on both wind and solar activity in the US while aggressively supporting fossil fuels and nuclear, alongside other renewables including biomass, geothermal, hydropower. Even energy storage has come in for a share of love from the Trump administration, further underscoring the remarkable exclusion of wind and solar from federal energy policy.

The trade organization Solar Energy Industries Association, for one, is urging members on both sides of the aisle to ensure that permitting reform focuses on fairness, predictability, and certainty. In a letter to the House and Senate, SEIA emphasizes that solar and storage developers “cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid.”

“According to researchers at Wood Mackenzie, solar and storage represent 70% of the new capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026. Yet $120 billion in clean energy investment is caught up in current permitting delays, let alone the impact of permitting challenges to future deployment,” SEIA adds.

Of course, even if such a bill passes both Houses of Congress, US President Donald Trump could exercise his veto power, and he has already threatened to make copious use of it during his last two years in office. Nevertheless, US Presidents come and go, and this one is scheduled to go in January of 2029 — peacefully this time, one hopes.

Assistant Secretary of Defense Dale Marks told a federal court that the Pentagon doesn’t have enough staff to review permits.

American Clean Power Association Vice President of Policy and Regulatory Affairs Tom Vinson disputed this in an Oct. 20 declaration, based in part on “information that ACP members provided to me.”

#5819. Martin Solar cuts out zip ties with new mounting rail

Martin Solar‘s newly manufactured Dual-Channel Solar Rail (DCSR) was recently installed on a 70-kWDC solar project, marking its first real-world application.

The Dual-Channel Solar Rail from Martin Solar.

“Management of PV wires and AC trunk cables is one of the most important aspects of rooftop PV installation. Anyone who has ever experienced running hundreds, thousands of feet of conductors on a rooftop system knows what a hassle it is having to apply countless zip ties that are not really suitable for long-term wire management,” said Preston Nelson, director of Martin Solar and co-inventor of DCSR. “What’s worse than the initial application of zip ties is having to pull up finished solar panels to apply even more zip ties after an inspector inevitably cites an installation for having wires that droop down to the roof surface.”

DCSR is designed with a wire trough large enough to fit three-phase trunk cables, like those manufactured by Enphase, Hoymiles, and AP Systems. It can also fit up to twenty standard PV cables, without the use of zip ties. Instead of using specialized panel clamps, DCSR’s panel attachment channel is off to the side of the wire trough, where it separately accepts panel hardware.

“The dual-channel design with separately dedicated features allowed us to increase the cross-sectional area of the wire trough to a size never seen before as a rail feature. In the past, we would install a separate wire tray to manage numerous long trunk cable runs, which was even more expensive and time-consuming. Now, this present project installation involves over 600 total feet of trunk, without a single cable tie. The separate wire trough can even allow access to wire runs without lifting panels, especially convenient when a worker simply needs to track a PV string,” Nelson said.

DCSR is the first product accessory to Martin Solar’s Hidden-Fastener Solar Mount, which mounts to the roof surface without putting holes in shingles. While Martin’s proprietary solar rail and mount can be paired, both are compatible with other solar racking and mounts.

Martin Solar will show DCSR and its solar mounting system at RE+ from November 17 to 19 at booth C5071.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5818. ConEd joins utilities seeking to loosen New York restrictions on owning generation

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company says reforms would boost renewables and help it achieve resource adequacy and environmental compliance targets.

Consolidated Edison, Inc. continues to plan for major infrastructure upgrades to meet a broad-based rise in electricity demand in New York City and state clean energy targets, according to the company’s regulatory filings and executives.

State law requires the state’s electric sector to reach 70% renewable energy by 2030 and fully decarbonize by 2040, despite amendments passed earlier this year that watered down some aspects of the law to “reflect the importance of feasibility, cost effectiveness and consumer affordability,” Jen Hensley, ConEd’s senior vice president of corporate affairs, said in an annual presentation for investors in October.

The company released third-quarter earnings on Nov. 5 but, as it has in recent quarters, did not hold a quarterly call to discuss its filing.

To boost system reliability while working towards the state’s clean energy goals, Con Edison has asked regulators to approve a new Reliability Asset Dispatch Rights (RADR) program aimed at distribution-level storage systems and extend a key deadline for adding transmission-connected bulk storage systems.

ConEd and its in-state peer companies have also proposed a framework for New York utilities to collectively develop and own up to 1 GW of land-based renewable energy projects annually, Hensley said.

That would mark a significant shift for New York’s restructured electricity landscape, where electric service companies like ConEd’s utilities generally do not own bulk generation and transmission. But it could help keep New York on track to meet its clean energy goals, Hensley said.

“We believe this would provide a long-term cost-effective strategy for supplying clean energy to customers, and we anticipate a white paper on this topic from the New York State Public Service Commission later this year,” she said.

Calls to ease restrictions on utility ownership of generation have grown in restructured U.S. markets with high power prices and development costs, despite pushback from independent power producers.

Earlier this year, for example, New Hampshire passed a law allowing utilities to own individual gas and nuclear generators under 5 MW capacity. Another New Hampshire bill that would have allowed utilities to own nuclear reactors under 300 MW capacity did not become law. The New York utilities’ proposal is more expansive than either.

With or without clearance for its three electric utilities to own generation, ConEd’s transmission subsidiary plans to make a significant investment in downstate New York’s power supply as a minority partner in the Propel NY Energy project.

The $3.26 billion joint venture with the New York Power Authority and other private developers would add three new substations, an underground transition vault and about 90 miles of underground and submarine 138-kV and 345-kV lines across western Long Island, parts of New York City and suburban Westchester County. The partners aim to finish work by mid-2030, pending state and local approvals.

Still, ConEd executives said more transmission, distribution and energy storage investment will be needed to keep the lights on in the coming years.

Consolidated Edison Company of New York, the ConEd utility serving the five boroughs and Westchester County, projects a capacity shortfall of 125 MW in New York City by 2033, rising to 675 MW by 2036 and 2,275 MW by 2045, Matthew Ketschke, CECONY’s president, told investors.

In July, CECONY filed a reliability contingency plan with state regulators that “includes market-based solutions, including procuring bids for additional transmission connected battery storage systems, creating a new distribution connected battery storage framework and issuing [a request for proposals] for non-storage clean and non-emitting technologies,” Ketschke said.

CECONY is “also planning for, but not seeking authorization for, transmission cooling enhancements that could increase transfer capability of generation from outside New York City by 300 megawatts,” he added.

Unlike other regions where near-term electricity demand growth is driven by large data center and industrial loads, ConEd sees more diffuse building and vehicle electrification driving growth in its territory. For example, new buildings’ electric demand requests are 20% to 25% higher than the historical norm for comparable structures, the company said last week.

ConEd did name a handful of new or expanded large-load customers set to come online soon, however: a new soccer stadium and entertainment complex adding 44 MW in Queens; a “construction and modernization” project adding 93 MW at John F. Kennedy International Airport, also in Queens; and an expanded Port Authority of New York and New Jersey bus terminal adding 42 MW in Manhattan.

As demand grows, ConEd utilities look for ways to increase system capacity without adding new substations, which Ketschke framed as a last resort.

“As the network grows beyond the capacity of the substation serving it, we divide the network in two and build a new substation to serve the new network, but not before we exhaust our toolkit of non-wire solutions, including demand management, battery storage and a host of other measures to avoid costly infrastructure investment,” he said.

But some new substations are inevitable. As a whole, ConEd says it will add 28 new electric substations over the next 10 years to the networks overseen by its electric utility companies, CECONY and Orange & Rockland Utilities.

CECONY, which serves the five boroughs and Westchester County, is in line for nine new substations. O&R, whose two electric utilities’ territories straddle the New York-New Jersey border west of the Hudson River, will get 19, the company said. Both projections are unchanged from the previous quarter.

ConEd’s three electric utilities took in a combined $4.4 billion in electricity revenue in the third quarter, up 8.8% year over year, the company said on Thursday. It’s the second consecutive quarter of strong electricity sales performance for ConEd. The company’s electric utilities grew sales revenue by about 10% year over year in the second quarter of 2026.

#5816. 300 Glaciers Have Disappeared from the American West Since the Mid‑20th Century — the Survivors Have a Few Things in Common

From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.

In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.

A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared, way more than I had anticipated.

Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise. Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places.

When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, like you’ll find in Alaska or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller.

We found that the average glacier area is about one-tenth of a square mile (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers).

I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate.

The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all.

We found the fastest-thinning glaciers are in the Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year.

It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, about half a foot of ice thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states.

In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits.

In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and found most would disappear by 2070 under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind.

The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question.

The principal importance of the glaciers is to provide water to high alpine ecosystems. The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain.

While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also contribute to hydropower production.

An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice.

High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat.

The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on.

By Andrew Fountain, Professor of Geography, Portland State University

#5811. Democrats Are at COP31 to Show That the US Has Not Abandoned the Fight Against Climate Change

The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 COP conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.

Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at COP is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the COP31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend COP summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.

Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at COP nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at COP with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

By Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Executives downplayed the potential for sweeping political change to impact the company’s strategy and growth plans. “I feel pretty confident about what we have in place,” CEO Chris Womack said.

Southern Co. could see its five-year capital plan increase to $100 billion on natural gas investments, nuclear uprates and additional generation, executives told investors and analysts during a third-quarter earnings call last week.

They also downplayed the potential for sweeping political change following the midterm elections to impact the company’s strategy, particularly with regards to large-load customers like data centers that are fueling its growth plans. Anger over energy costs, including electricity bills, helped Democrats seize control of Congress and many state leadership positions, including in Georgia, where they won the governor’s office and a majority on the Public Service Commission.

“I feel pretty confident about what we have in place,” CEO Chris Womack said.

He said he has not heard “any talk about retroactive” data center freezes or “looking backwards” at signed contracts.

“We have strong confidence in ... what we've done in the contracts that we signed that are in place and are in effect,” Womack said.

David Poroch, the company’s executive vice president and CFO, said even if development slows down and data centers don’t ramp as quickly as expected, its contracts contain provisions for minimum bills that cover at least 100% of the cost being introduced into the system.

“Before the kilowatt moves over the meter, we are recovering our costs embedded in those minimum bills,” Poroch said. “So we've kind of disengaged ourselves from the need for a customer to achieve their ramp rate for us to recover our cost.”

Womack also listed several large loads that are not data centers, which he said will continue to fuel economic growth in the South, including projects from Airbus, Mitsubishi Power, Audi and others. Mitsubishi Power plans to greatly expand its gas turbine manufacturing facility in Savannah, Georgia, helping meet rising power generation needs, he said.

In the third quarter, the company's Georgia Power subsidiary also received approval for an agreement with Google to expand nuclear capacity through uprates over the next several years, said Poroch. The company is also bidding on new generation contracts in Alabama and Georgia, he added.

“To the extent potential company-owned resources are selected through these processes and ultimately authorized by the respective [regulators], this could represent substantial incremental investment, together with opportunities for additional investment across all our businesses,” Poroch said.

In response to an analyst’s question, he said he expects more than 90% of new investment to target state-regulated projects versus competitive power markets and interstate pipelines.

In the third quarter of 2026, retail electric revenues were $6.6 billion compared to $5.7 billion for the corresponding period in 2025, and $16 billion year to date compared to $15.1 billion in 2025, according to its quarterly filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The company attributed the increase to changes in rates and pricing, and higher contributions from commercial and industrial customers.

Southern saw weather-normalized electricity sales across all customer segments rise 3.5% in the third quarter and 2.7% year to date, led by commercial sales, which were up 7.3% compared with the third quarter of 2025.

“This large load customer demand is translating into increasing usage,” Womack said. “Notably, data center usage was 59% higher this quarter and is now up 52% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from data center customers.”

He said the company’s portfolio of signed large-load contracts has grown to 21 GW with an additional 7 GW in late stages across Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi.

“Now, are we going to land 75 GW of projects? Probably not,” said Womack, referring to the company’s speculative pipeline. “I mean, we'll continue to risk adjust it, but I think it's a clear indication and a demonstration of the interest in our territory.”
