#5757. Michelle Yeoh Says Window Seats Are Underrated, And She's Right (That You Should Leave The Aisle Seats For Me)

By definition, hot takes are supposed to be controversial. If everyone agrees with your hot take, it's probably a lukewarm take at best, because that's how kids decided the slang worked. Kareem Rahma has taken advantage of this with Subway Takes, a show where he sits on the New York subway and records people's hot takes. This week, Oscar-winning actress Michelle Yeoh made an appearance and decided the hill she would die on is that window seats are underrated. A lot of people won't like it, but you know what? She's right.

Flying is a miracle of engineering and modern manufacturing. We literally built machines that defy the will of the gods, zoom across our skies, and let us travel in ways we were never meant to travel. Should I have been able to pull off a whirlwind visit to Boston while living in Georgia? Probably not, but the miracle of flight made it possible, and there's always going to be some thing special about sitting in a window seat that lets you see the beautiful world beneath you. Los Angeles isn't the prettiest city in the world, but even LA looks incredible from 10,000 or 15,000 feet.

With the window seat, you'll also have an easier time napping on your flight, and air travel takes so much time out of your day, you could probably use a snooze. Yes, most seats now have those bendy headrests that are supposed to make napping a little easier, but nothing beats using a sweater as a pillow and leaning against the plane. The bendy headrests can try, but while they're better than nothing, they still don't work all that great. All humans need to sleep, so book a window seat, enjoy the view, and then take a nice nap once the plane makes it above the clouds.

Does going to the bathroom get a little awkward? Sure, but there's no reason you have to drink four whiskey cokes before you board your flight. They have edibles for that now. Any time you get up to go to the bathroom, that's also the opportunity to make a new friend. Most importantly, if everyone who reads this ends up fighting over those beautiful views from the window, there will be more aisle seats available for me to take. Michelle may have a point, but I still prefer the aisle and will not be changing my mind.

#5755. Your Holiday Gifts Don’t Have To Be Delivered By Diesel

The 2026 holiday shopping season is soon to be upon us, with gift buyers and bargain hunters perusing stores in person and online. Behind the scenes, the US freight system has been working hard to transport the goods and gifts, traveling mostly by truck as they make their way through ports, warehouses, and highways.

So, what effect will the rising price of gasoline and diesel fuel have on the year’s biggest shopping season? The historic shock in prices at the pump has driven cost increases for the goods consumers buy throughout the economy, including holiday gifts, because costs to produce and ship goods have increased. Between January and October, the average national price for a gallon of diesel rose nearly 80 percent.

But it doesn’t have to be this way. The trucks moving and delivering goods throughout the economy don’t have to be subject to the high cost and volatility of the fossil fuel market. Globally, businesses are transitioning their fleets to zero-emission trucks. In addition to their public health and environmental benefits, zero-emission trucks (and battery-electric models in particular) offer significant reductions in operating costs compared to those powered by fossil fuels. This can help protect producers and consumers from expensive and volatile fuel prices and unhealthy air.

That can help us all breathe a bit easier.

This year’s holiday shopping season is marked by several unsettling trends—record high fuel prices and the second-largest monthly jump in the Producer Price Index (PPI) since 2010, as well as the largest 12-month increase in the PPI since 2022. This jump in the PPI, the measure of the costs incurred by US businesses to make, ship, and sell their goods, was meaningfully driven by the single largest month-to-month increase in producer energy costs in the past decade and a half. Additionally, September 2026 saw the third largest increase in transportation and warehousing costs under the PPI since 2010, only behind April 2026 and March 2022—the months following the beginning of the current US-Iran conflict and Russia’s war on Ukraine, respectively.

While Santa’s reindeer are primarily fueled by carrot snacks during the holiday season, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, the rest of our nation’s freight system is most often powered by dirty and increasingly expensive fossil fuels. In September, diesel fuel prices hit record highs—topping as much as $9 per gallon at some retail gas stations. Diesel-fueled trucks are the workhorse of the US freight system, carrying more freight by weight than all other transportation modes combined. Each year, tractor trucks consume over 27 billion gallons of fuel, and fuel is the second-largest cost input to trucking after labor.

Higher fuel costs can ultimately be passed along to consumers and contribute to higher price variance for goods. This is particularly the case with certain food prices. A 2023 study in Energy Economics found that fuel price shocks accounted for nearly 20 percent of the price variance of cereals. Unfortunately, this means that even the reindeer aren’t immune to fossil fuel volatility.

Consumers may never see a fuel surcharge listed on a holiday gift, but fuel costs are embedded throughout the supply chain. When diesel prices spike, it becomes more expensive to move products between ports, warehouses, stores, and homes, even for carriers that hedge fuel prices through bulk or futures fuel agreements. Powering more of those trips with comparatively stable electricity can reduce one source of sudden cost pressure before products reach shopping carts.

Battery-electric trucks can provide far greater fuel cost predictability while also offering significantly lower per-mile fuel costs than fossil-fueled trucks. Between January 2016 and September 2026 (the most recent data month at the time of this publication), annual diesel price volatility averaged 3.75 times that of commercial electricity prices, according to our analysis of Federal Reserve and Energy Information Administration data. During this time, diesel prices saw a monthly spike of greater than 10 percent seven times, including four times in 2026. Diesel prices between February and March 2026 saw the highest price spike by far at over 32 percent. By contrast, the highest spike in the national average commercial electricity price in the last decade was 4.4 percent.

While it’s true that both diesel and electricity prices have increased this year, the magnitude of those increases is hardly comparable. Between January and September, the average national price for a gallon of diesel fuel rose nearly 80 percent compared to just two percent for average commercial electricity rates.

Consumers are paying for these higher petroleum prices at the pump and checkout lines, while oil companies and shareholders are seeing a windfall: both ExxonMobil’s and Chevron’s Q3 2026 earnings were more than double those of Q3 2025.

But the costs of our fossil fuel-powered freight system extend far beyond our wallets.

Fossil-fueled medium- and heavy-duty trucks are also the nation’s largest source of smog-forming pollution and account for the largest share of the nearly 10,000 premature deaths associated with transportation pollution in the US each year, despite making up just 13 percent of the vehicles on our roads.

Trucks are a particularly significant source of pollution in areas near the warehouses and logistics centers that our holiday packages travel through. For the 66 million people living near freight corridors, warehouses, ports, and railyards nationwide, the price of a fossil fuel-powered freight system is too often paid for with their health. Recent UCS research found that the 1.7 million people living near 10 or more freight facilities face a cancer risk from air toxics that is 32 percent higher than the national average.

While freight operators cannot control geopolitics and fuel prices, they can control which fuels they choose to use. Increasingly, freight operators are considering the switch to electric trucks, which offer more stable and affordable fueling costs with far less exposure to volatile global oil markets. FedEx, for example, recently announced plans to add 2,000 electric delivery trucks to its growing zero-emission delivery fleet.

The economics for zero-emission trucks are increasingly compelling—this is partially why we’ve seen continued adoption of electric commercial vehicles despite the current federal leadership’s best efforts to prolong our reliance on fossil fuels. Even states not typically thought of as electrification front-runners have seen meaningful growth in zero-emission delivery vehicles. In 2025, over 17 percent of new commercial vans in both Mississippi and Louisiana were zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs). In Georgia, nearly 35 percent of new commercial vans registered last year were electric.

California continues to lead the nation in overall deployments of zero-emission medium-and-heavy-duty vehicles, with zero-emission models accounting for over 24 percent of all new vehicle registrations in 2025. While this is a slight backstep from 2024 levels, California continues to see growth in the deployment of zero-emission tractor trucks. In California, ZEVs comprise around 8 percent of new tractor trucks registered in 2025, and it appears the momentum is just getting started. In the first three quarters of 2026 alone, California fleets applied for state clean truck incentives for more than 1,000 new electric tractor trucks—a clear example of growing interest and demand.

Momentum toward tractor truck electrification is picking up in other parts of the country as well. In September, Catalyst Mobility, a leading clean transportation nonprofit, announced that a group of major businesses, including Microsoft and Pepsi, placed a combined order for 2,500 battery-electric Tesla Semis—the largest single order of zero-emission trucks in US history. These trucks can travel up to 500 miles on a single charge at maximum legal capacity and regain 60 percent of range in a 30-minute charge. Earlier this year, Pilot Travel Centers announced a partnership with Tesla to install high-speed chargers for electric semi-trucks across major freight corridors in California, Georgia, Nevada, New Mexico, and Texas. The first of these stations is now operational.

Despite impressive momentum, private investments and market forces alone are unlikely to reliably electrify our freight system at the needed pace. The freight industry continues to face widespread adoption barriers, including higher upfront costs for many zero-emission truck models and lack of access to widespread, reliable commercial truck charging infrastructure. At the same time, consumers have limited ability to choose shippers committed to cleaner freight. We cannot simply toggle a “green delivery” option when shopping at a local store or online.

That’s where public policy comes in: to reduce barriers to electric truck adoption and accelerate the transition toward a cleaner, more affordable freight system.

At a time when the federal government’s support for freight sustainability and modernization has reversed and is undermining previous progress, state and local governments have the opportunity and responsibility to adopt and implement policies and programs that build momentum toward an electrified freight system. Specifically, they should accelerate zero-emission truck deployment where it is technically and economically feasible today, while addressing the technological and economic barriers that limit adoption elsewhere.

Policies and programs that drive electrification today while addressing barriers could include those that:

This holiday season, millions of gifts will move through a vast network of trucks, warehouses, and distribution centers before we give them to friends and loved ones. Increasingly, those trucks don’t have to run on diesel. Electric trucks offer a path toward a freight system that produces less pollution while reducing business and consumer exposure to the volatile global fossil fuel market.

However, widescale freight electrification is unlikely to occur at the pace needed without effective public policy. Smart public policies and programs can accelerate electric truck deployment where it already makes the most economic and environmental sense, while tackling the costs and infrastructure challenges that remain.

Consumers don’t always have the option or transparency to choose cleaner freight, but we can push our elected representatives to pursue policies and programs that deliver a more sustainable way to move the economy.

If you’re an early-career scientist, seasoned scientist, or technical expert, you can join our science network for opportunities to advocate for smarter transportation policies.

#5754. Advances and Unmet Needs in Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease

— It's better care that has led to better survival, not new treatment options

As the 1970s came to a close, sickle cell disease (SCD) remained largely a pediatric condition because few children born in the U.S. with the condition survived to adulthood. Today, about 95% of children born with SCD in developed nations survive to adulthood. Median life expectancy in the U.S. has reached 60 years, meaning half of all patients live to that age, as compared with less than 40% just 10 years ago.

The dramatic improvement in survival evolved from an amalgamation of factors including universal screening of newborns, prophylactic penicillin to prevent bacterial infections, immunization against Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and broader and better-informed use of FDA-approved therapies for SCD. A recent multi-article review covered some of the key developments, as well as ongoing challenges and unmet needs.

Ironically, a clinical trial that did not meet its primary endpoint has profoundly influenced management of SCD. The randomized, placebo-controlled BABY HUG trial failed to show that hydroxyurea reduced the risk of kidney and spleen damage by 50% in very young children with SCD. Nonetheless, the trial showed that patients randomized to hydroxyurea had significantly fewer SCD-associated clinical events, including pain, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, blood transfusion, and hospitalization. Investigators concluded that hydroxyurea "can now be considered for all very young children with sickle cell anemia."

BABY HUG was a landmark clinical trial because of the history of hydroxyurea, which was initially approved only for adults with SCD who met specific high-risk criteria. Published more than a decade ago, the trial established clinical principles that remain highly relevant today for children with SCD.

"[BABY HUG] gave us the evidence that hydroxyurea can be used as prevention, so before kids start having all these complications," Allison King, MD, MPH, PhD, of Washington University in St. Louis, told MedPage Today. "BABY HUG was really helpful because instead of being so reactive, the practice could be very proactive in pediatrics."

A recent analysis of more than 2,000 children with sickle cell anemia treated with hydroxyurea established long-term safety and efficacy. Children followed for as long as 8 years had significantly fewer and briefer hospitalizations, and laboratory data showed sustained improvement in hemoglobin in patients with good treatment adherence.

The Silent Cerebral Infarct Transfusion trial, published more than a decade ago, also had a transformative impact on SCD management. The results, in 200 children with sickle cell anemia, showed that regular blood transfusions significantly reduced the risk of silent cerebral infarction, which can have more subtle neurologic effects as compared with a stroke.

"A lot of our kids, and adults, have cognitive deficits, which are kind of like invisible disabilities because [the patients] can be quite verbal but have significant attention problems, processing speed, executive function that limit their ability to progress in their daily activities," said King. "Also, silent infarcts are a high risk for having overt strokes. Now it's an evidence-based guideline that we should be screening, as well as responding and transfusing, to prevent the progression."

Fast forward a decade and gene therapy became the next transformative clinical development in SCD, offering the potential for cure. Unfortunately, other therapeutic options for SCD have remained limited throughout the decade. One of the approved drugs, voxelotor (Oxbryta), was withdrawn from the market after post-approval data analysis and real-world clinical experience showed the benefits no longer outweighed the risks. Concern has arisen about the future status of another approved agent, crizanlizumab (Adakveo), which lost its conditional European marketing approval. Additionally, the drug failed to outperform placebo for reducing episodes of vaso-occlusive crisis in a recent phase III trial.

Moreover, cost and access remain major obstacles to expansion of gene therapy as a treatment option. In 2025, fewer than 200 patients worldwide received the two gene therapies, which come with a hefty price tag of $2-$3 million. Additionally, the process for screening and preparing patients for gene therapy can be "laborious" for many families, said King.

Despite the advances, more and more effective therapies are an ongoing need for patients with SCD, said Ofelia Alvarez, MD, of the University of Miami Health System.

"There is still a lot to do," she told MedPage Today. "The most widely used medication, hydroxyurea, does not work for all children with sickle cell anemia. Some patients do not respond. They continue to have low hemoglobin despite the treatment. We need new therapies to improve anemia, to decrease complications. They are always in need."

Better transitional care also has contributed to better survival in SCD. However, the quality of care and the ability to provide good transitional care vary greatly. Transition involves much more than handing off a patient from pediatric care to adult care, said Alvarez. Most young patients need to be educated about the disease itself, what medications are available and how they are used, and how to make appointments. Some need to learn about practical issues, such as budgeting, transportation, and learning to live independently.

"Here at the University of Miami, we have a very robust program that is co-created with patients and explained to the parents," said Alvarez. "After the transition, we follow up with the patients to see how they feel about the process and whether they have become integrated into the [adult] practice... . I personally don't have a lot of problems because I work very closely with the adult providers."

In some settings and circumstances, transition into adult care can be complicated and anything but a smooth process. The age at transition varies from practice to practice, but 18 is a common age. King, who specializes in caring for children, has expanded her patient age range up to 26. She described a 23-year-old patient whose circumstances are not rare in the SCD community.

"He has been intermittently homeless for 2 years," said King. "In his words, he 'couch surfs.' He doesn't have a stable place to live. He's not sure where he's getting his food. His meds are always being stolen, so he's frequently in the hospital for pain."

The case also illustrates the problem with using pain as a patient-reported endpoint for judging treatment efficacy, which has been a historical standard for the FDA.

"Pain is so multifactorial," said King. "It could be just sickling, and I'm not trying to minimize that, but it could be very biologically driven, but often, particularly in older teens and adults, psychosocial factors really are big drivers. That makes it difficult to tease out what's really driving a patient's pain."

Finding the origin of a patient's pain has been complicated by the fact that "for the last 20 years, we were sort of crawling our way out of the opioid crisis," said Jeffrey Glassberg, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"When I was in med school, we were taught that there was no danger to opioids," Glassberg told MedPage Today. "If you're treating pain, no harm could come to the patient. Today, I think most people who treat a lot of sickle cell patients would agree: Opioids cause pain. Full stop."

"We have noted that the more opioids that we were giving over the last couple of decades, the more pain our patients would experience, and that pain is non-vaso-occlusive," he continued. "Our latest research is really finding that patients feel that the pain is identical to vaso-occlusive crisis ... The more opioids you give, the more pain that patients will experience that's non-vaso-occlusive, but feels the same."

A number of candidate drugs for SCD have failed to pass muster with the FDA because they did not show a reduction in vaso-occlusive crises. Moving away from that as an endpoint for efficacy and toward a more objective endpoint -- such as organ damage -- might increase the likelihood of more drug approvals and more treatment options for patients, said Glassberg.

#5753. Computer vision startup Tristar AI pulls in $12.4M to automate quality control for manufacturers

All too often, manufacturing defects seem to slip past human eyes, with the result that high-speed production lines turn into expensive scrapheaps. Computer vision startup Tristar AI Inc. has just raised $12.4 million in early-stage funding in order to try to put an end to these costly mistakes.

Today’s Series A round was led by Isogon Ventures and saw participation from Blackhorn Ventures, Ford Street Ventures, NextView Ventures, TenOneTen and Capgemini’s ISAI Cap Venture Fund.

Tristar AI is gearing up to transform quality assurance in manufacturing at a critical moment for the industry. Manufacturers have found themselves squeezed by a combination of rising raw material costs and growing labor shortages, and these problems have been made even more acute by the U.S. government’s insistence on bringing more manufacturing back home.

According to data from the Capgemini Research Institute, 48% of U.S. companies have invested in reshoring projects this year. But 83% say they’re worried about the lack of skilled industrial workers needed to fulfill those initiatives.

One of the major challenges for manufacturers is that they’re still encumbered by inefficient inspection protocols that rely on either manual checks, or in a best-case scenario, rigid, rule-based machine vision systems. Quality control is essential for any manufacturing operation, but the inefficiency of these protocols makes it a significant roadblock too.

It forces companies to take skilled workers off production lines and sometimes even bring their entire operations screeching to a halt. Yet there are many occasions where they still miss subtle flaws in their products, resulting in wasted materials, downtime, missed deadlines and sometimes even very expensive customer claims.

Founder and Chief Executive Salem Karani is all too familiar with the inefficiency of manual inspection. He told SiliconANGLE that while growing up, he would often accompany his father to his family’s plastic film manufacturing plant in Houston, turning up at all hours of the day and night in order to troubleshoot production issues that could spring up at any moment. Because the company’s margins were so tight, any period of extended downtime could threaten its profitability, so he would spend hours with his dad frantically troubleshooting line errors.

It was this experience that ultimately inspired Karani, who studied computer vision at Harvard and MIT, to develop an automated quality inspection system that can operate continuously without slowing down production. “The problem was never that people didn’t care about quality,” Karani said. “It’s that people catch problems after the fact, once they’ve already cost time, materials and customers. Tristar gives every production line a live record so teams can act when it matters most.”

Computer vision in manufacturing operations is not a new concept, but where Tristar differs is through its use of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models that can adapt to changing conditions, materials and defect types. The startup’s platform looks at machine telemetry, the quality of the products coming off the line and the activity of human operators, allowing it to uncover issues the moment they emerge and immediately understand where the problem is, and why it occurred.

Best of all, the system can integrate with factories’ existing systems, such as cameras, sensors, programmable logic controllers, enterprise resource planning systems and so on That enables them to get up and running without an expensive overhaul.

Isagon Ventures General Partner Paco Riberas said he’s backing Tristar because manufacturers are losing far too much money to avoidable defects. “In today’s industry, precision isn’t optional, and Tristar makes it possible,” he said. “Its AI vision catches defects in real time, directly on existing production lines. Salem and his team are building the quality standard for modern manufacturing.”

Tristar’s early traction has been encouraging. Its system already monitors more than 500 production lines across North America and Europe.

Customers include global packaging giants such as Amcor, DuPont and Klöckner Pentaplast, and also some of the biggest suppliers to automakers such as Toyota, Honda and Mercedes, Karani said. Those customers report defect detection accuracy rates of between 95% and 99%, and say the platform pays for itself in an average of just four months.

Karani said the goal now is to expand Tristar’s platform into new manufacturing sectors and enhance the capabilities of its computer vision AI to try and improve its accuracy even further. Ultimately, he sees the company as the operational system of record for factory floors, giving manufacturers more visibility into everything about their production operations, from the raw materials to the finished product.

“Physical AI will play a critical role in the future of manufacturing,” said Capgemini Ventures’ Matthieu Eyriès. “Tristar combines advanced AI capabilities with a strong understanding of industrial environments, addressing concrete manufacturing challenges with measurable impact.”

The Mississippi River is partially closed after a tanker ship t-boned and sank a docked riverboat with approximately 129 passengers and crew members on board in the Port of New Orleans at approximately 12:30 p.m. ET on Friday. City officials said an estimated 32 people have been transported to nearby hospitals with non-critical injuries, and all passengers are now accounted for, miraculously confirming no casualties from the tragedy. The exact number of injuries caused in the collision is not currently known, as it remains an active and evolving incident. The collision happened outside 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, and the U.S. Coast Guard closed the Mississippi River to all vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96.

The American Cruise Lines' American Heritage riverboat was docked for about two hours to begin passenger disembarkation when the Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with it. WDSU News said, "Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel are on scene, conducting rescue and response operations." Their rapid response is being called "a miracle on the Mississippi."

Louisiana Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser told ABC News he was worried about the victims because these type of river cruises tend to draw elderly passengers. WDSU said rescued passengers are being brought into the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triage and assistance. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said the water temperature near the shipwreck is about 66 degrees, which is cold enough to potentially cause hypothermia if a person is exposed to it for too long.

There is no confirmed cause of the crash, though it is suspected to be due to a loss of steering. After the initial impact, the riverboat began taking on water and capsized very rapidly, and it is now resting on its side at the dock. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry rushed to the scene and said he spoke with President Donald Trump about the crash, who told him he had any support he needed. The U.S. Coast Guard is now working on reopening the river, and it is working with salvage assistance teams to salvage the vessel and remove it from the area.

#5751. Hydropower Generation in the Southwest Fell to Record Lows This Summer

Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey.

Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows.

However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years.

We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won’t eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity.

According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region’s generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.

#5750. 1970 Dodge Challenger R/T For Sale With 96,199 Miles Shown Wraps 440 V8 In Plum Crazy Purple

It wasn't that long ago that a different, clean, Plum Crazy 1970 Dodge Charger caught our eye on the used market, but there's now a Challenger R/T from the same year and painted the same color available. Apparently, we like Purple around here. Spotted on Hemmings Classified is a 1970 Dodge Challenger R/T with 96,199 miles on the odometer. The seller, Ryle's Rides in Sacramento, California, is asking $69,995 for it.

Per the factory fender tag, this one was originally powered by a 383-cubic-inch Magnum V8 engine paired to a four-speed manual gearbox. But somewhere along the way, somebody dropped a 440 big-block V8 from 1969 into it instead.

This motor gets an aluminum intake manifold, four-barrel carburetor, chrome valve covers, and an upgraded aluminum radiator to help keep it cool. The four-speed manual gearbox remains, albeit rocking a pistol-grip shifter. #5749. Response to Standard PBC Treatment at 1 Year Linked to Lower Long-Term Risks

— "Response predicts outcomes in real-world care, and nonresponders carry a risk," researcher says

A biochemical response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) at 12 months was associated with lower 5-year risks of hepatic decompensation and mortality in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), a propensity-matched landmark cohort study suggested.

Among patients considered to be responders -- defined as an alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level ≤130 U/L and a bilirubin level ≤1.0 mg/dL -- the 5-year cumulative incidence of hepatic decompensation was 10.2% versus 17.8% among nonresponders (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.51-0.70, P<0.001), reported EzzElDien A. Ibrahim, MD, MSc, of the University of Missouri in Columbia, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

In addition, the cumulative incidence of 5-year all-cause mortality was 12.2% among responders versus 16.3% for nonresponders (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.84, P<0.001).

Other clinical outcomes also trended in favor of or significantly favored responders:

"Response predicts outcomes in real-world care, and nonresponders carry a risk," Ibrahim said. "We can check ALP and bilirubin at 1 year on UDCA," and at that point, clinicians should consider "escalating nonresponders without delay."

UDCA is the first-line treatment for PBC, a rare and chronic autoimmune disease of the bile ducts, "and it ... works," Ibrahim noted.

An international cohort study that included 3,902 patients from the Global PBC Study Group database showed that after inverse probability treatment weighting, the 10-year cumulative liver transplant-free survival rate was 79.7% among UDCA-treated patients and 60.7% among untreated patients, with UDCA treatment resulting in a statistically significantly reduced risk of liver transplant or death (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.40-0.52, P<0.001).

However, 20% to 40% of patients do not respond biochemically to UDCA at 12 months. In 2024, seladelpar (Livdelzi) and elafibranor (Iqirvo) were granted accelerated approval for patients with PBC who either did not respond to UDCA or were intolerant to the treatment.

While a number of criteria such as the PARIS criteria link 12-month response to UDCA to outcomes, Ibrahim said real-world validation in routine care for 5-year clinical endpoints -- such as decompensation and death -- is limited.

This explains "why this study matters," he noted.

For this study, Ibrahim and colleagues used the TriNetX U.S. Research Network that includes data on 147.5 million patients from 112 health systems.

They included matched cohorts of 2,911 patients with PBC. Mean age was 61.3, 87% were women, 77% were white, 34% had a cirrhosis code, 14% had portal hypertension, and mean albumin level was 3.86-3.91 g/dL.

Responders and nonresponders to UDCA were categorized based on propensity score matching of 29 covariates that included demographics, liver and mental health comorbidities, alanine aminotransferase levels, aspartate aminotransferase levels, platelet counts, albumin levels, and international normalized ratio.

Ibrahim acknowledged that the study had a number of limitations, including the fact that PBC was defined by codes and not by a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody test or histology. In addition, there was no access to UDCA dose or adherence data, and there were a limited number of 5-year events for the liver transplant and hepatocellular carcinoma analyses.

— Veterans groups, psychedelic advocates say the drug has great promise for mental heath conditions

Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers, and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.

The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose, and design studies of the drug.

Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors, and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy, and most other psychedelic drugs.

Veterans organizations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression, and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.

Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.

"That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process," Kennedy said. "We're going to have, I think, a record drug approval process."

Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.

Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and "best-in-class research."

"For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce," Collins said.

Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.

Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.

Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the FDA. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.

Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.

The little data currently available mostly come from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.

Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: "Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let's do it."

#5746. With $23M in funding, Luminal is the latest startup to put Nvidia’s CUDA moat in its crosshairs

Luminal AI Inc. has outlined a plan to tear down Nvidia Corp.’s formidable software moat in the artificial intelligence chip industry after raising $23 million in early-stage funding.

Today’s Series A round was led by Standard Capital and saw participation from existing investors such as Y Combinator, SagaVC, Liquid 2 and Felicis, bringing Luminal’s total amount raised to date to more than $28 million. It comes about a year after the startup raised $5.3 million in seed funding.

Everybody knows about Nvidia these days. The chipmaker has ridden the generative AI wave to a staggering $5 trillion market valuation, surpassing rivals such as Apple Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. to become the most valuable publicly traded company in the world. But anyone who assumes that it’s solely Nvidia’s graphics processing units that set it apart would be mistaken, for the real reason for its dominance of the AI computing industry is not just silicon, but software.

For almost two decades, Nvidia’s proprietary Compute Unified Device Architecture or CUDA software framework has been the real differentiator, serving as a virtually impenetrable barrier that prevents rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Google LLC and Amazon Web Services Inc. from stripping away its market lead. Though those rivals have developed some very powerful GPUs and custom application-specific integrated circuits for running AI workloads at lower costs than Nvidia’s hardware, they haven’t been able to match the scale of Nvidia’s software ecosystem.

Virtually every major AI framework, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, has been built natively on Nvidia’s CUDA software, enabling developers to run their AI models on Nvidia’s GPUs without any modifications. But to run their models on alternative chips, developers need to rewrite much of the underlying code, which is challenging and time-consuming work. That’s why the vast majority of AI workloads still run on Nvidia’s chips.

Many developers don’t want to be paying the exorbitant fees needed to rent Nvidia’s GPUs or purchase them outright, but they also don’t want to spend months at a time fine-tuning their codebases to get their AI models to run optimally on alternative hardware, and it’s this challenge that Luminal intends to solve for them.

The startup’s solution is a two-pronged architecture platform that consists of its proprietary search compiler and a fully managed inference cloud that combine to eliminate the hassles of bringing AI workloads onto different chips.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Joe Fioti told SiliconANGLE that the compiler works by systematically exploring different ways of running neural networks on the target chip in order to come up with the most optimal path. It benchmarks each variation until it finds the best possible solution, and then it automatically generates the code developers need.

Once the code is ready, it caches the implementation so it can be reused across recurring inference workloads. In this way, it allows developers to run their AI applications across heterogeneous chip architectures with minimal fuss, Fioti said.

“We started out building in the open on GitHub as AI adoption took off, and quickly saw how much demand there was for a more efficient way to run AI models across different hardware,” Fioti said of the company’s origins.

Luminal’s compiler and inference cloud are designed primarily for running high-throughput, continuous-uptime AI applications that demand massively scalable inference. Think applications such as AI coding tools, automated image generation engines, AI video generators and real-time voice agents.

“The cost of running AI shouldn’t limit who gets to build it,” Fioti said. “We’re building the infrastructure to make high-performance inference more accessible, giving developers more choice beyond Nvidia’s ecosystem without forcing them to compromise on speed or cost.”

Luminal launched its compiler and public cloud-based inference infrastructure just four months ago and adoption is growing rapidly. It’s already processing more than 45 trillion tokens per month – a number that’s roughly equivalent to 10% of the total tokens consumed so far by Together AI Inc., an $8 billion-valued infrastructure unicorn that has been serving the market for more than four years already. The startup has established a strong partnership with AWS, and runs a significant amount of its workloads on that company’s Tranium processors.

Going forward, Luminal’s plans include expanding its engineering team, scaling its go-to-market operations and optimizing its compiler and inference infrastructure to support more chip hardware and AI models.

Standard Capital’s Dalton Caldwell said he’s betting on Luminal because AI inference is the fastest-growing market in the world. “We backed it because of its deep technical expertise and its demonstrated proof that it can squeeze fantastic performance out of heterogeneous hardware,” he said. “Luminal’s ability to get the most out of GPUs that have already been purchased … is incredibly high leverage.”

Though Luminal has had a promising start, it’s certainly not the only company trying to break Nvidia’s CUDA stranglehold on the AI industry. Both Google and AWS have their own things going on, notably launching alternative AI frameworks to PyTorch that make it easier for developers to create AI models and applications that can run on their native processors.

Luminal also faces competition from startups such as Spectral Compute Ltd., which offers a programming toolkit and compiler that enables CUDA-based code to run natively on any AI-accelerated chip. There are also open-source efforts such as the UXL Foundation’s OneAPI, which converts CUDA code into software that can easily run on any silicon.

#5744. Prescriptions Down 25%, Overdoses Cut in Half: What Stopped a Gabapentinoid Surge?

— Study identifies three interventions that may have influenced pregabalin use

High-profile media coverage of the harms associated with the gabapentinoid pregabalin (Lyrica) and tighter safeguards coincided with fewer prescriptions and overdoses in Australia, a retrospective study showed.

Following a media campaign, tighter dispensing rules, and boxed warnings, pregabalin prescriptions and overdoses dropped significantly below projected trends -- falling by 25% and 47%, respectively -- reported Rose Cairns, PhD, of the University of Sydney, and co-authors in The BMJ.

This was a reversal from a steep upward trajectory that had persisted since 2013, the researchers noted. The shift corresponded to ongoing monthly reductions in prescriptions of 0.7% (95% CI 0.5-0.9) and in poison center overdose calls of 1.6% (95% 1.0-2.3).

Australia historically has had a big problem with pregabalin use and overdose, and many other countries face similar issues, Cairns noted.

"Importantly, the interventions that were associated with a decrease in harms included things like raising public awareness of the risks via the media and boxed warnings. These relatively 'soft' interventions can still have an impact," she told MedPage Today.

The findings are "really positive, but we think use of pregabalin is still far too high," Cairns continued. "There's a lot of off-label use for conditions with minimal evidence to back that up. And while high-risk use has decreased, we really need to continue to minimize co-use with opioids, which has been shown to increase the risk of death."

Gabapentinoids -- pregabalin and gabapentin -- were originally developed as antiseizure drugs. Subsequent indications have expanded to include neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and fibromyalgia.

"Despite this relatively narrow range of approved indications, gabapentinoids are considered 'blockbuster' drugs," Cairns and colleagues wrote. "High-income countries have the highest rates of gabapentinoid consumption, while low- and middle-income countries have had the highest consumption growth in recent years. Most of this consumption is driven by off-label use for non-registered indications."

In the U.S., pregabalin is scheduled under the Controlled Substances Act. Gabapentin is not scheduled at the federal level but eight states have enacted legislation to classify gabapentin as a schedule V controlled substance.

In 2019, the FDA warned that respiratory depression or death may occur in patients taking pregabalin or gabapentin with opioid pain medicines or other drugs that depress the central nervous system. Despite this, co-prescribing of gabapentinoids and opioids persists.

In the U.K., one-third of substance use deaths involve a gabapentinoid, predominantly pregabalin, and deaths involving gabapentinoids have more than doubled from 2018 to 2022, Cairns and co-authors noted.

The study in Australia is "timely and rigorous, but these figures warrant caution," noted David Juurlink, MD, PhD, of the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto, in an accompanying editorial. "The ecological design cannot establish causation, and poison center calls are an imperfect measure of poisoning incidence, influenced by reporting practices and patterns of healthcare use," he pointed out.

Pregabalin should be used more selectively, Juurlink argued. "Although it can provide meaningful relief in some patients with neuropathic pain or fibromyalgia, most do not achieve substantial pain relief," he wrote.

"For other painful conditions, the evidence is even less encouraging," Juurlink added. "Randomized trials and meta-analyses have found no convincing evidence of benefit for low back pain or sciatica, conditions for which the drug is nevertheless frequently prescribed. Pregabalin's commercial success, in other words, has far outstripped its demonstrated clinical utility."

To evaluate pregabalin use and misuse in Australia, Cairns and colleagues evaluated dispensing claims and poison center overdose data from 2016 to 2024, focusing on three key events: widespread media reporting about the harms of pregabalin in December 2018, tighter prescribing restrictions after April 2020, and the introduction of boxed warnings in February 2021.

The researchers randomly sampled 10% of Australians with drug subsidies and 50% of calls placed to the country's largest poison control center. During the study period, 227,864 people were dispensed 3,441,851 pregabalin prescriptions, and 4,871 pregabalin overdose calls were reported.

Use and overdoses peaked in 2018 before plateauing and declining. Dispensing dropped significantly at three time points: in December 2018 (corresponding to high-profile press coverage), in May 2020 (after tighter prescribing restrictions were introduced), and in December 2021 (after boxed warnings were in effect).

The findings are observational, the researchers acknowledged. The study analyzed subsidized prescriptions only and poisons center data may be subject to reporting bias, they added. The researchers also could not determine patients' access to pain treatments.

Color Health, a virtual oncologist-led cancer clinic, has announced formal clinical collaborations with 10 National Cancer Institute-designated cancer centers.

Cancer is among the top drivers of healthcare costs and mortality. Because of its complex and variable nature, the quality and timeliness of care are the best ways to improve outcomes and manage costs. That means less duplicate testing, fewer treatment changes later and fewer avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations.

Among the collaborating centers are City of Hope-Los Angeles, Memorial Sloan Kettering, Moffitt Cancer Center, Mount Sinai, Stanford Medicine Cancer Center, UC Davis Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated cancer centers go through a robust evaluation for meeting quality, safety and access standards.

When care at a specific center is determined to be a good fit for a patient, Color coordinates directly to match patients with the right team, completes the clinical workup, reviews medical records and completes authorizations to each center’s specifications. First-appointment targets for most patients are set at seven days or fewer for oncology referrals placed by Color Medical. Additionally, Color verifies insurance coverage to ensure the referral is in-network. Occasionally, Color works with payers or centers on single-case agreements if something is otherwise out of network.

“Color is, above all, a very patient-centered company. When an individual faces a cancer diagnosis for the first time, Color helps to provide the information and navigation to top cancer centers. Their process balances technology with a human touch,” Karen Lu, M.D., physician in chief at Moffitt Cancer Center, told Fierce Healthcare over email.

For any patient issues, Color clinicians escalate to the collaborating centers. Patients also get ongoing wraparound support from Color during and after treatment, including nutrition, mental health, palliative and survivorship care. Additionally, Color will collaborate with the centers to identify any potential clinical trial candidates, gather the needed information and support institution-led eligibility assessment and enrollment.

UCSF Health has already worked with Color for years, so the latest collaboration is an expansion of the partnership.

“They’re all seeing, obviously, rate increases," she said. "The disease space and the market is very active."

Color partners with local providers to clinically manage all patients through its oncologist-led care team. Its virtual cancer clinic is a national center of excellence certified by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, meaning it meets rigorous standards and is subject to annual audits and reviews. The company, which started working in the cancer space in 2023, says its patients see 66% faster diagnosis and a 77% increase in screening adherence. #5742. Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day

Eating mango and avocado every day could offer unexpected benefits for heart health, according to new research. In a study lasting just eight weeks, adults with prediabetes who regularly ate both fruits experienced improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, without gaining weight or consuming more calories.

The findings could be especially relevant to the one in three (98 million) Americans with prediabetes, a condition in which blood sugar levels are elevated but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, the research suggests that incorporating these two nutrient-rich fruits into everyday meals may help support cardiovascular health.

Researchers at Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) investigated the effects of an Avocado-Mango (AM) diet that included one medium Hass avocado and one cup of fresh mango each day. Participants followed this eating plan for eight weeks, while a comparison group consumed a similar diet in which the fruits were replaced with carbohydrate-based foods containing equivalent calories.

The results revealed notable differences between the groups, particularly in how well their blood vessels functioned and how their blood pressure changed over time.

One of the clearest improvements involved the ability of blood vessels to expand as blood flows through them. This flexibility helps maintain healthy circulation and is an important indicator of cardiovascular health.

To evaluate this response, researchers measured flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a commonly used test of endothelial function (blood vessel health). The endothelium is the thin layer of cells lining the inside of blood vessels, where it helps regulate circulation and the widening and narrowing of arteries.

Among participants eating avocado and mango, the measurement increased significantly to 6.7%. In contrast, it declined to 4.6% in the control group. The difference suggests that regularly consuming these fruits may help blood vessels function more effectively.

Blood pressure measurements also showed encouraging changes, especially among male participants. Men in the control group experienced an average increase of 5 points (mmHg) in central blood pressure, while those consuming avocado and mango saw a reduction of approximately 1.9 points.

Diastolic blood pressure, the lower number in a blood pressure reading, reflects the pressure inside arteries when the heart relaxes between beats. Maintaining healthy levels is important because elevated blood pressure can place additional strain on the cardiovascular system. Researchers noted that the differences observed in the study could be clinically meaningful if they persist over time.

Importantly, the cardiovascular improvements occurred without significant changes in participants' body weight or total calorie consumption. This suggests that the nutritional quality of the foods people eat may influence heart health even when their weight remains stable.

“This research reinforces the power of food-first strategies to help reduce cardiovascular disease risk, particularly in vulnerable populations like those with prediabetes,” said Britt Burton-Freeman, PhD, Principal Investigator and Professor at Illinois Tech. “It’s an encouraging message: small, nutrient-dense additions—like incorporating avocado and mango into meals and snacks—may support heart health without the need for strict rules or major dietary overhauls.”

Beyond the improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure, participants eating mango and avocado consumed more fiber, vitamin C, and monounsaturated fat. These nutrients are associated with cardiovascular wellness and may help explain some of the observed benefits.

Researchers also identified improvements in certain indicators of kidney health, including estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), a measurement used to assess how effectively the kidneys filter waste from the blood.

However, the fruits did not produce significant improvements in every health measurement. Cholesterol levels, blood sugar, and markers of inflammation remained largely unchanged compared with the control group.

Together, the results suggest that regularly including nutrient-rich fruits in the diet could be a practical way to support cardiovascular health, particularly for people with prediabetes who face an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Although mango and avocado have very different flavors and nutritional profiles, they provide complementary nutrients that support several aspects of cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Mango provides dietary fiber (2g/serving, 7% DV, Mango serving size: ¾ cup) and is an excellent source of vitamin C (50% DV). Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage, while fiber contributes to healthy digestion and may help with blood sugar regulation, weight management, and cardiovascular wellness.

Avocado offers another combination of potentially beneficial nutrients. It contains fiber (3g/serving, 11% DV, Avocado serving size: 50 g (1/3 of a medium avocado)), which plays a role in managing cholesterol, blood sugar, and body weight.

It also supplies unsaturated fats (6g unsaturated fats), which can support heart health by helping reduce LDL cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol, when they replace less healthy fats in the diet. Additionally, avocado contains potassium (250mg, 6% DV), a mineral involved in regulating blood pressure.

By providing fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and potassium, mango and avocado offer a convenient way to increase the nutritional value of everyday meals. However, the study did not establish whether eating the two fruits together provides greater benefits than consuming either fruit separately.

Incorporating these fruits into meals does not require a complicated eating plan. Their contrasting flavors and textures make them useful ingredients in salads, smoothies, and grain bowls.

For example, fresh mango can add sweetness to a savory dish, while avocado contributes a rich, creamy texture. Both can be used in recipes such as Mango Avocado Tuna Ceviche or an Avocado and Mango Topper.

Additional recipes and nutritional information are available at Mango.org and LoveOneToday.com.

The investigation included 82 adults between the ages of 25 and 60 who had prediabetes and were classified as having overweight or obesity (BMI 25–35 kg/m2). All participants were generally healthy, did not smoke, were not following specialized diets, and had no major chronic medical conditions.

Over eight weeks, participants followed calorie-controlled eating plans modeled on typical American dietary patterns. One group ate a medium Hass avocado and a cup of fresh mango daily, while the control group received carbohydrate-based alternatives with comparable calorie content.

To make the comparison as consistent as possible, researchers prepared and supplied meals covering 75% of each participant's estimated daily calorie needs. Participants chose their remaining foods independently, allowing some flexibility while helping the researchers limit differences between the two diets and encourage adherence.

The primary measurement was flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a noninvasive method for assessing how effectively blood vessels respond to increased circulation. Researchers also examined blood pressure, blood sugar, and other metabolic indicators, inflammation, kidney function, and dietary nutrient intake.

Despite the additional fruits, the avocado and mango group did not experience significant changes in body weight or overall calorie intake. This finding suggests that incorporating nutrient-dense foods into an otherwise balanced diet may improve certain aspects of cardiometabolic health without necessarily contributing to weight gain.

The study had several strengths, including its carefully controlled feeding approach, two parallel comparison groups, and emphasis on whole fruits rather than isolated nutrients or supplements.

However, researchers also acknowledged important limitations. The intervention lasted only eight weeks, so it remains unclear whether the improvements would persist over months or years. The participants also represented a relatively narrow population of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, meaning the findings may not apply equally to people with different health conditions or dietary habits.

The research measured cardiovascular risk indicators rather than long-term outcomes such as heart attacks or strokes. Larger and longer studies will be needed to determine whether the observed changes translate into lasting reductions in cardiovascular disease risk.

Nevertheless, the findings offer an encouraging indication that relatively modest changes in food choices may benefit blood vessel health, even without weight loss or a major dietary overhaul.

This study was supported through an unrestricted grant from the National Mango Board (NMB) and the Hass Avocado Board (HAB). NMB and HAB had no role in the study design or findings.

Compliance automation company Vanta Inc. today launched AI Governance by Vanta, a product on its Agentic Trust Platform said to give security teams a single view of every artificial intelligence system in a company.

Also making their debut at VantaCon 2026 in San Francisco this week are Risk Quantification, Autonomous Vendor Assessments and a new version of the Vanta Agent that the company claims can take on entire jobs.

Vanta is pitching the new products at security teams that are under pressure to move faster on AI. According to job-title data compiled by Vanta, the number of AI security engineers and architects has tripled so far this year compared with all of 2025.

AI governance roles, which did not appear in the company’s figures before 2024, have grown tenfold in two years. A complete inventory of the AI tools in use is still out of reach for many security teams, Vanta said.

Point products for AI security often detect threats without the business context to judge how much they matter, according to Vanta. The company claims to be the only vendor tying an AI agent’s live security telemetry directly to an organization’s compliance controls.

#5740. Major Change to Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines

— ACS now recommends PSA testing every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69

Shifting gears on prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society (ACS) now recommends screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69.

Since the release of its previous guideline 16 years ago, the ACS had recommended that average-risk men consult with a physician before deciding for themselves whether to undergo a screening PSA test.

The new ACS recommendations also strengthened guidelines for men at high risk for prostate cancer, recommending annual screening beginning at age 45 for Black men and those with a strong family history of the disease. The organization previously recommended that those men discuss the pros and cons of screening with a physician at age 40 or 45.

The changes reflect the accumulation of stronger evidence that screening PSA tests reduce prostate cancer mortality and diagnosis of late-stage disease, according to the updated guidelines from Robert Smith, PhD, ACS senior vice president for early cancer detection science, and colleagues, appearing in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians.

"We've just reached a point in our understanding of prostate cancer, especially that [screening] can reduce the risk of being diagnosed with metastatic disease and dying of prostate cancer," Smith told MedPage Today. "We have good protocols for avoiding harms."

Smith noted that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not updated their prostate cancer screening guidelines since 2018. For average-risk men, the USPSTF recommends discussion-backed decisions on PSA testing for men ages 55 to 69.

"I cannot tell you what [their recommendations] would be if they updated them today, but they did not have the data in 2018 that we had in 2025 with the update of the European trial data showing the endurance of the mortality reduction," said Smith.

The update aligns with recent evidence supporting PSA screening for prostate cancer as "one of the most important steps men can take to protect their health," said Ash Tewari, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"We have strong evidence that PSA testing can reduce the risk of dying from prostate cancer, and advances in MRI and other diagnostic tools are helping us identify potentially dangerous cancers while avoiding unnecessary procedures," he said. "Knowing your risk, getting screened regularly, and having these conversations early can save lives."

With the update, the ACS takes a clear position on prostate cancer screening, said Mark Ashamalla, MD, of Episcopal Health Services in New York City.

"For years, the ACS largely focused on encouraging men to discuss the pros and cons of PSA screening with their doctors," said Ashamalla. "Now they're taking a much clearer position and actually recommending regular screening. For men at average risk, that means a PSA blood test every 2 years between ages 50 and 69, while Black men and those with a strong family history should begin annual screening at age 45. This is a significant shift and reflects growing evidence that regular screening can reduce the risk of advanced prostate cancer and save lives."

"The goal isn't to find and treat every prostate cancer," he added. "It's to catch the dangerous ones early enough to make a difference. I think that's the biggest takeaway from these new guidelines."

By way of the guidelines, the ACS also recommends:

The updated guidelines are supportive of the recent trend toward active surveillance as the primary option for men with low-risk prostate cancer.

"It's important to recognize that prostate cancer screening has evolved over the past 30 years," said Smith. "More and more people appreciate that very worrisome harms associated with therapy can be avoided, especially if a man is diagnosed with prostate cancer that is not aggressive. Active treatment should be avoided until such time as it appears that the disease has become aggressive. Some men may be diagnosed with a prostate cancer that's not very aggressive, and they will live with it in that state for the rest of their lives. [They can] avoid harms that are quite diminishing to quality of life."

"On the other hand, if a man's prostate cancer becomes more aggressive, and treatment is necessary, then the process of active surveillance will at least have postponed it for a number of years, allowing men to not have to live with those [treatment-related] side effects," said Smith.

#5739. Hims & Hers reports $890.4M Q3 revenue, tightens 2026 outlook

Hims & Hers reports $890.4M Q3 revenue, tightens 2026 outlook" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Digital health and wellness company Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue outlook after missing Wall Street analysts’ revenue and earnings estimates.

Andrew Dudum, co-founder, chairperson and CEO, pointed investors toward the increasing scale of Hims & Hers' pharmacy and lab infrastructure. That growth is driving efficiencies for the company, as is its artificial intelligence-native experience, he said.

“That infrastructure positions us to launch treatments of increasing complexity, including testosterone replacement therapy this quarter and our Peptides Plus offering later this month,” Dudum said.

Peptides have been a focus for the company as of late, with Dudum telling investors last quarter it plans to offer already-permitted peptides, like sermorelin and NAD+.

Dudum said that Hims & Hers’ long-term strategy focuses on “three critical commitments:” being a leader in metabolic health domestically and globally, leading major markets globally and being "at the forefront of category expansion.”

“Each of these reinforces the other, and together they describe how Hims & Hers becomes the global destination for consumer health,” he said. “We are investing aggressively against all three because this opportunity is growing quickly, and we believe it will become more valuable every quarter.”

The company reported $890.4 million in revenue in Q3, up 49% compared to revenue of $599 million the year prior, according to financial results published Monday. Net loss was $33 million, compared to $15.8 million in profit for the same quarter a year ago.

Chief Financial Officer Yemi Okupe said that revenue excluded $18 million from the “scaling of membership revenue” in the company’s weight loss offering but will be recognized in the fourth quarter.

“This revenue deferral has no impact on free cash flow generation,” Okupe noted.

Adjusted EBITDA was $82.4 million compared to $78.4 million the year prior.

Ethan Feller, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research, told Fierce Healthcare the company’s revenue was “roughly what Wall Street expected,” adding that U.S. “growth sped up to 21%.”

“But the company lost 14 cents a share against an expected gain of six cents, its third big miss in a row,” Feller said. “It is also keeping less of each sale, as gross margin fell to 57%, down from 74% a year ago, as more of the business shifts to lower-margin brand-name weight-loss drugs.”

Feller added that the company’s “growth story is still a real long-term tailwind.”

“Demand for weight-loss drugs is strong, and having both Novo and Lilly on the platform helps,” Feller said. “But as long as margins keep shrinking, the stock will likely stay under pressure until either the price falls to a level that reflects the lower margins or the company shows it can turn a steady profit.”

As a result, Hims & Hers tightened its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $3.13 billion to $3.15 billion and reduced its adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $257 million to $277 million.

“This is a reflection of the more aggressive strategic pricing and marketing actions that we expect to take in the U.K. and Germany, and the weight loss membership deferral noted above,” Okupe said.

The earnings report comes on the heels of an announcement that the company struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer its branded obesity treatments directly through the Hims & Hers platform. The drugs were previously only available to patients if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

“Nearly 3 million people across four continents rely on us to access care,” Dudum said. “That trust has made us a valuable partner to global pharmaceutical leaders like Novo and Lilly, and positions us to keep bringing the most innovative treatments to our customers as they come to market.”

Dudum added that the company is planning to launch “flexible multi-month subscriptions” across its assortment to make it easier for customers to address health goals.

“We will continue to prioritize partnerships across the industry, with the goal that whenever an innovative therapy reaches the market, our customers can access it here,” Dudum said. “That assortment will sit alongside an AI-native experience that will soon be available to nearly every weight loss customer on our platform.”
