Haupert will stick around through 2027 in an advisory role to soften the transition, support philanthropic and capital fundraising and provide strategic guidance on a new $1+ billion medical campus the nonprofit also announced this week.

Haupert has headed Grady for the past 15 years. Saul has been around for seven, initially joining as chief financial officer.

> AI-powered prior authorization company Humata Health is bringing Liz Fowler, former director of the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), onto its board of directors.

The company said in an announcement that Fowler's experience at CMMI will support the team's efforts to accelerate Humata's mission to ensure patients get the care they need quickly. At CMMI, Fowler was tasked with rethinking reimbursement in Medicare and Medicaid to drive uptake of value-based care, providing critical insights she can bring to Humata.

Before her stint at CMMI, Fowler held leadership roles at the Commonwealth Fund and Johnson & Johnson. She currently serves as a distinguished scholar at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the Carey Business School.

“Liz is a unicorn, a rare leader with deep experience in all realms of the healthcare ecosystem,” said Jeremy Friese, M.D., Humata’s co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “She understands the inherent complexities of the health system, and her expertise will be instrumental as we work toward our mission of solving these challenges."

From her role driving innovation at CMMI to her track record of bipartisan work on federal health legislation, Liz’s experience will be an invaluable asset as we make AI-driven medical review a seamless process that ensures every patient receives the right care as quickly as possible," Friese said.

> Jeff Balser, M.D., Ph.D., is retiring from his roles as CEO of Vanderbilt Health and dean of Vanderbilt University School of Medicine at the end of 2026.

The academic system's board of directors has kicked of a national search for a successor who would hold both titles, according to the March 12 announcement.

A 1990 Vanderbilt graduate himself, Balser spent years as a cardiac anesthesiologist and surgical intensivist at Johns Hopkins before returning to Vanderbilt in 1998. He was named chair of the Department of Anesthesiology in 2001, dean of the medical school in 2008 and head of the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in 2009. He has served as dean and in the health system's top executive role for the past 17 years.

The organization has grown from a four-hospital system to an eight-hospital system under his tenure, during which its annual net revenue also grew from around $2 billion to nearly $9 billion, according to the announcement. Part of that time was an effort he led to legally and financially separate the medical center and its system from the university as a standalone nonprofit. The organization's cash reserves also have also grown from 50 days to more than 110, with total cash on hand plus investments now exceeding $3 billion.

> Greg Hoffman, chief financial officer of Providence, will retire in June, the organization announced.

Hoffman has been with the major nonprofit system for over a decade, and served as CFO for the past five years. His tenure in the role is marked by a multi-year financial turnaround that finally brought operations into the black during the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2025. The announcement of his retirement also pointed to his role striking up new strategic partnerships, resetting contracts with commercial payers and heading the implementation of an enterprise resource planning system.

Providence said it plans to conduct an internal and national search for Hoffman's replacement.

> Kevin Tabb, M.D., president and CEO of Beth Israel Lahey Health, has given notice to the system's board that he plans to step down after this year.

The physician executive was tapped as CEO of Beth Israel Deaconess in 2011, and stayed at the top through its merger with fellow Massachusetts provider Lahey Health in 2019. Today the organization spans 14 hospitals, employs 42,000 people and cares for 1.7 million patients annually.

Alongside navigating the merger and a pandemic, Tabb is credited with advancing initiatives around care access and connecting services delivered between its locations. Beth Israel Lahey also notched new partnerships: a teaching relationship with UMass Chan School of Medicine and an upcoming cancer collaboration with the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Tabb will remain in his role while the system's board searches for his successor, a process expected to take about eight to 10 months, according to the announcement.

> Health tech company Stellar Health has added Raul Smith, a veteran of Elevance Health, as its chief financial officer.

Smith has 20 years of experience in healthcare leadership, according to an announcement, including six years as president CFO for Anthem's East Region. He has also served as CFO for Duo Health and Gold Kidney Health Plan.

Stellar said that Smith's experience in the health insurance industry will help the company build out its platform. Stellar supports payers in value-based care by making it easier for providers to engage with these complex environments.

In addition, he'll play a key role in driving the financial evolution of its risk-based portfolio, including the tech-enabled accountable care organization, shaco.

"Stellar is already setting the pace for value-based care, and Raul adds the institutional caliber to match our growing scale," said Michael Meng, CEO and cofounder of Stellar Health. "Raul brings the financial authority to stand behind the definitive value we deliver to our payor partners. His leadership solidifies that our ROI is absolute and verifiable—impact that will only continue to compound and get better year over year."

> Wellpoint Tennessee, an Elevance Health subsidiary, has named Rachel Chinetti as president of its health plan.

As president, Chinetti will be tasked with leading the insurer's strategy and operations across the state, including a focus on affordability, access and quality for individuals enrolled in TennCare, its Medicaid program.

She brings almost two decades of experience in Medicaid and long-term services and supports (LTSS) to the role, per an announcement from the insurer. Chinetti has held multiple roles within TennCare and most recently served as a staff vice president within Elevance Health's government unit, where she led a center of excellence in LTSS.

Chinetti is also a native of the state who lives in Nashville, with strong community relationships, the company said.

“It is an honor to serve Tennesseans in this role,” Chinetti said in the release. “Wellpoint Tennessee has a strong legacy of partnership and innovation. I look forward to working alongside TennCare, providers, advocates, and community leaders to strengthen rural and maternal health, enhance long-term services and supports, and deliver more coordinated, person-centered care that helps our members live healthier, more independent lives.”

> James Downing, M.D., will be stepping down from his role as president and CEO of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital near the end of 2026, the pediatric research hospital announced.

The physician executive has been with the organization for four decades, and has sat at its head for the past 12 years. Under his leadership St. Jude underwent the largest strategic expansion in its history, which included the completion of two separate strategic plans requiring nearly $20 billion of investment and over 2,300 new positions; major expansion to St. Jude's main campus; and greater international collaboration.

Prior to that he served as scientific director for eight years, a period in which he spearheaded the Pediatric Cancer Genome Project.

Downing plans to transition into a faculty role at St. Jude's Department of Global Pediatric Medicine after handing over the reins. The organization said a replacement is expected to be named over the summer.

“I’ve watched St. Jude transform the care of pediatric cancer around the world, and I’m grateful to have played a small part as its CEO," he said in the announcement. "It has been the honor of a lifetime to wake up every day and know that I have a purpose, to be a part of this workforce, and to change the outlook for children everywhere.”

>The Department of Health and Human Services announced several leadership changes as the agency looks to advance Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Make American Healthy Again agenda.

HHS said that Chris Klomp will step into the role of chief counselor at the agency, where he will "oversee all operations of the department." Klomp currently serves as the director of Medicare.

In addition, both Politico and the Washington Post have reported that Jim O'Neill, deputy secretary of HHS and the acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, will step down from both roles. Sources told the Post that O'Neill will be offered a position as an ambassador.

The Post reported that the shakeup comes amid significant controversy over the shift at HHS in vaccine policy and other hot-button topics. Kennedy is looking to shift talking points to more politically palatable topics, like healthy food, per the Post.

In addition to the new title for Klomp, Kennedy has tapped Kyle Diamantas and Grace Graham to serve as senior counselors for the Food and Drug Administration as well as John Brooks to step in as senior counselor for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

HHS said that each of these three will also continue to hold their current roles in addition to supporting Kennedy's office.

"I am proud to elevate battle-tested, principled leaders onto my immediate team—individuals with the courage and experience to help us move faster and go further as we work to Make America Healthy Again," Kennedy said in the press release.

>The Federation of American Hospitals announced multiple leadership appointments this week.

The organization's new CEO, Charlene MacDonald, took the role on Jan. 1, and on Jan. 14, FAH revealed the names of key members of her team, including:

McBride brings more than 25 years of overall healthcare experience to the COO role, including more than four years at FAH as its leading voice on patient safety, quality and public health. Broder has been at FAH for more than two years, and will take on an expanded role as chief strategy officer, spearheading efforts to support the organization's mission as well as its long-term stability and growth.

Keefe joined FAH in December 2024 and has more than two decades of policy experience, both at the state and federal levels. Tenoever will continue in the general counsel role, and has held similar titles at other trade associations, FAH said.

“Our exceptional new executive team will be integral to the Federation’s success as we write our next chapter,” MacDonald said in the announcement. “We’re at a critical moment for health care coverage and access, and our team’s proven ability to be strategic, nimble, and relentlessly solutions-oriented will allow the Federation to deliver for our members and the millions of patients they serve.”

>Eduardo Conrado stepped into the CEO chair at Ascension on Jan. 1, taking over for the retiring Joseph Impicciche.

Conrado has been the major health system's president since 2023, and continues to hold that title. He joined in 2018 to serve in digital, strategy and innovation positions. Prior to that, he’d spent 26 years at Motorola Solutions and served on Ascension’s board for five years.

In a blog post published this week, Conrado said his focus as CEO will be for Ascension to strengthen access to care, modernize care delivery and deepen commitments to those most in need—achieved through a combination of mission-driven strategy, capital deployment and talent.

>Jesse Ehrenfeld, M.D., has joined clinical AI company Aidoc as its new chief medical officer.

Ehrenfeld, a board-certified anesthesiologist and clinical informaticist, steps into the role after a stint as president of the American Medical Association. There, he led advocacy on issues like physician wellbeing and the responsible use of AI in clinical care. His new post will keep to those subjects as he supports Aidoc's health system customers.

“It’s clear that Aidoc’s success to date has been rooted in building technology physicians trust," he said in a release. "I’m joining to help scale that impact, ensuring that clinical AI continues to be a seamless, essential part of the modern care delivery model.”

>Abhi Rastogi took on the roles of president and CEO at Temple Health on January 2, taking over for Michael Young, who retired.

Rastogi has been with the organization for more than 20 years. He most recently served as the president and CEO of Temple University Hospital and its campuses, as well as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the broader system. He's credited with delivering more than $100 million in annual impact via operational and financial improvements.

>Christian Pass was named chief financial officer of Keck Medicine of USC, and will officially begin the new role on Jan. 12.

He comes to the academic health system from Optum, where he was president of provider and payvider enterprise clients. Before that he had several senior financial leadership titles at John Muir Health that culminated in a chief financial officer role.

“Pass has more than 30 years of health care finance leadership experience with a proven history of cultivating high-performing teams and guiding organizations through critical financial and operational transformations,” Rod Hanners, CEO of Keck Medicine, said in a release. “He brings tremendous knowledge and skill to this position that will support the continued growth of the health system.”

>Sarah Ness officially began her new job as president and CEO of PeaceHealth on Jan. 3.

Ness has been with the nine-hospital system for more than 20 years, most recently as its executive vice president and chief administrative officer. She's credited with leading organizational transformations within the system's culture, technology systems and operations.

She takes over for Liz Dunne, who had announced her retirement last year.

>Chip Hubbs, the president CEO of Marysville, Ohio-based Memorial Health, shared plans to retire at the end of this year.

He's held the roles for nearly 22 years, and before that was the CEO of Community Memorial Hospital elsewhere in the state. "In all, Chip has worked for nine different hospitals throughout his career in every facet from groundskeeper and maintenance to intern, fellow, Evening Administrator, Executive Director, and CEO," according to the announcement.

Hubbs plans to work with the health system's board on a long-term strategy and transition plan during his final year in the office.

>The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the lobbying group representing pharmacy benefit managers, has named longtime policy expert David Marin as its new CEO, succeeding J.C. Scott.

Marin will officially take the CEO chair on Jan. 20, according to a PCMA announcement. He comes to the organization from drugmaker Viatris, where he was the global head of government affairs, public policy and advocacy. He also previously served as a managing principal at Podesta Group, where he led advocacy efforts for a slew of firms including the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association and Mylan.

He also held key staff roles on the Hill, according to the announcement.

“David Marin is the ideal leader for PCMA at a time of significant change in our industry,” said PCMA Board Chair Adam Kautzner, President of Express Scripts and Evernorth Care Management.

In addition to Marin's hire, PCMA announced that Brendan Buck will serve as the organization's new chief communications officer, also effective on Jan. 20. Buck joins PCMA from public affairs firm Seven Letter.

#5666. Brain implant startup pauses trials

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Annalisa Merelli and O. Rose Broderick

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Buongiorno! Today’s stories have me wondering what it must be like to study the human brain: Every new discovery is a breathtaking revelation, and also a reminder of how little we know, and how far the horizon of full understanding still is. It feels a little like looking at the universe, only what is infinite is, in the most literal sense, ourselves.

For many teenagers, phones are pervasive — and destructive. And the policy proposals and scientific research meant to address the crisis are moving too slowly to help a generation already hooked on screens.

But as STAT’s Isabella Cueto reports, a variety of homegrown initiatives are filling the gap, many of them led by teens. Some programs draw inspiration from Alcoholics Anonymous, helping teens develop tools and strategies to refocus and put their devices away. Others are pushing teens to understand the financial incentives behind holding their attention. The techniques are as varied as they are creative: public interventions, manifestos, and overall a movement that is reclaiming attention, real life connections and, ultimately, freedom. Read all about it here.

Biomarker-based diagnostics have improved our understanding of who may develop severe dementia, advancing our knowledge of Alzheimer’s disease and the hope of finding effective early treatment.

Yet for the people who become aware of their heightened risk, the knowledge is bittersweet. The information allows them to act by taking drugs that may delay dementia onset, but it also carries a weight. In a new First Opinion, Neurotransmissions columnist Jason Karlawish shares how learning of elevated risk changed people’s outlook on the future, from bucket lists to plans for care, to considerations about assisted suicide. (And in case you missed it, check out the first installment in this miniseries here.)

The basal ganglia is a gumball-sized region of the brain so central to psychiatric and neurologic conditions that one scientist called it “the Grand Central station of disease.”

Now a massive scientific collaboration has created a map of the area, including a list of which cells are present and how they arranged. This research has led to the discovery of a new type of neuron, and the identification of cells linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Authors consider it a “monumental achievement” that opens the door for understanding the brain in health and disease, but further progress may be at stake amid government funding cuts, Jonathan Wosen reports.

When STAT’s Megan Molteni started investigating the experimental reproductive procedure known as MRT, or mitochondrial replacement techniques, she didn’t know that she would uncover a sprawling international network of clinics that that market to older women.

Over the course of her reporting, she also found evidence that MRT can effectively treat age-related infertility is lacking. In fact, data obtained by STAT shows MRT doesn’t work for patients of advanced maternal age.

Read more of her takeaways from this eight-month investigation here. And if you haven’t already read Megan’s original investigation, I encourage you to dig in.

Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation brain-computer interface. The Brooklyn-based startup’s device was a wireless version of its first-generation device, which snakes a catheter through veins to park a stent near the brain’s motor cortex. The aim was to connect users to digital devices using brain activity. The pause is not safety related, leaders said.

It’s the first major hiccup for Synchron, one of the leading companies in a fast-growing industry aimed at helping people with disabilities like ALS and paralysis regain independence through brain implants. Synchron will also eliminate jobs in New York City and is working to develop a new device, WIRED reported.

The news gives context to a cryptic comment CEO Tom Oxley gave on a conference panel in New York City last week. “There are hundreds of components in our system, and it just takes a delayed one to slow down your submission to the FDA,” said Oxley, flanked by his competitors at Neuralink and Precision Neuroscience. “We had one particular component that we were caught up on.” – O. Rose Broderick

Come January, Abdul El-Sayed will be the first epidemiologist in the Senate. His election comes as the U.S. is struggling through a spike in measles cases, a Dengue fever outbreak, and a recent foodborne illness crisis.

STAT’s Nick Florko spoke with the senator-elect about how he hopes to rebuild trust in science, as well as who’s responsible for the current state of affairs. “We didn’t have to get here,” El-Sayed said. “In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information-mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame … our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.” Read the whole meaty interview here.

#5665. Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong earnings results

Shares of artificial intelligence cloud operator Nebius Holdings NV dropped 17% today after it posted third-quarter financial results.

The company’s adjusted profit and revenue topped expectations. The selloff may have been sparked by its full-year forecast, which fell short of the consensus estimate. It’s also possible the sudden departure of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed. Nvidia is an investor in Nebius and many other AI and cloud companies.

Another possible factor: Nebius increased its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion. According to CNBC, that’s $4.15 billion higher than what Wall Street had expected. The company’s plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year surpassed the consensus estimate by an even wider margin.

The surging expenses may be related to its shift away from colocation facilities. Today, about 90% of the company’s infrastructure is located in rented data centers. In contrast, the next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity that it plans to bring online will be mostly powered by internally operated data centers.

“Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term,” said founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh. “We will continue to invest across the business – in our capacity and infrastructure buildout, in our platform and products, and in the team that takes this to market.”

Nebius swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year ago to a $90.9 million adjusted profit. The latter figure breaks down to adjusted earnings of 31 cents per share. The company’s profitability surprised analysts, who expected a loss of 69 cents per share.

Revenue growth was another bright spot. Sales jumped 517% year-over-year, to $980.8 million, which put the company well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus estimate.

One of Nebius’ main growth drivers is its Token Factory service for running open-source AI models. Developers use it to host both post-training and inference workloads. Nebius says that the offering, which launched a year ago, is nearing a “multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate” after logging a 17-fold quarter-over-increase in contract value.

Nebius’ largest customers played a particularly important role in its strong quarterly performance. The company signed $12 billion worth of contracts in the three months ended Sept. 30. The haul included multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and other major tech firms.

The company uses customers’ contract prepayments to finance its data center projects. The company says that the value of the prepayments it received in the third quarter exceeded its capital expenditures. However, the ratio of prepayments to capital expenditures is expected to decline as Nebius ramps up its data center spending. That detail may be yet another factor in today’s stock selloff.

Nebius expects its full-year revenue to be “at the low end” of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range. Analysts expected $3.37 billion. For 2027, Nebius is forecasting $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue.

#5664. Ardent Health acquiring Missouri nonprofit Boone Health for $47M

Ardent Health acquiring Missouri nonprofit Boone Health for $47M" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Ardent Health is acquiring Boone Health, a mid-sized nonprofit system based in Columbia, Missouri, for $47 million in cash, the organizations announced Thursday. It marks Ardent's first entry into the Missouri healthcare market.

The deal, expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, includes a 10-year, $200 million capital commitment on nonprofit Ardent’s part. That money will be invested in Boone’s facilities, workforce and, in the near term, an expansion of its emergency department, according to the announcement.

Ardent has agreed to maintain Boone’s essential hospital services while developing its 392-bed regional referral center, Boone Hospital Center. It also plans to maintain employment for existing Boone employees and providers, continue its charity care policy and establish a local advisory board.

“We are acquiring a strong asset in an attractive and growing midsize market with significant opportunity to drive operating and financial improvement, all while delivering high patient quality care and safety,” Ardent Health President and CEO Dave Caspers said during a Thursday afternoon investor call discussing the deal. “It also represents an effective use of capital at a compelling valuation that we expect will create long-term shareholder value.”

Alongside its main hospital, Ardent would acquire Boone’s medical group, 19 care sites including an outpatient campus and five medical office buildings, related ancillary services and real estate. The system is the second-largest provider in its region with about 30% market share and half a billion dollars of annual revenue, Caspers said, with a local population that is well insured (93% coverage) and growing well ahead of the national average (3.4% in the next five years).

“Boone expands our footprint into a new attractive market,” Caspers explained. “It diversifies our business and enhances scale. Further, adding Boone's regional system to our portfolio is consistent with our strategy of building leading healthcare platforms in growing mid-sized communities. We're highly aligned with Boone Health on culture and mission, including putting the patient at the center of everything we do, with an aim toward best-in-class clinical care, patient quality, safety and access to services.”

The executive noted to investors that Boone’s facilities are relatively modern and well maintained, allowing Ardent to direct more capital toward its growth. The company has also identified “meaningful opportunities to optimize financial performance.” By leveraging its larger scale and expertise to tackle costs (supply chain procurement, vendor consolidation) and revenue cycle processes, Ardent executives said they expect to generate about $5 million to $10 million additional EBITDA within the deal’s first year, and at least $30 million of annual synergies three years after the deal’s close.

Boone Health has been independent since 2021, following over three decades during which it operated as part of the BJC HealthCare system. In 2025, its leadership kicked off a search for potential strategic partners “that could provide additional capital and resources to support the system's continued growth. Ardent was selected after a comprehensive evaluation process led by an independent advisory firm,” according to Thursday’s announcement.

“In Ardent, we identified a partner that supports our mission, respects our culture and can accelerate our vision without compromising what makes Boone Health special,” Jerry Kennett, M.D., chair of Boone’s Board of Trustees, said in the announcement. "Following a thoughtful review, the Board is confident Ardent is the right long-term partner for Boone Health. This agreement protects what our community has built while giving Boone Health the resources it needs to grow."

Ardent Health’s current operations include 30 acute care hospitals and over 280 care sites, several of which are run as part of a joint venture structure with other health system partners. In 2025, the company increased its revenues by 6% to $6.3 billion and grew its adjusted EBITDA to $545 million.

The company recently logged a strong third quarter off the back of solid demand for emergent care and progress on its ongoing performance improvement initiative. In September, it also officially divested from a joint venture with the University of Kansas Health System, a decision that leadership said is part of an ongoing review of its portfolio to ensure long-term strategic fit among its hospitals and partnerships.

#5663. A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease

A natural substance found in broccoli could offer an unexpected new approach to treating a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system. Researchers at Swinburne University have identified promising effects from the compound, raising hopes for a more affordable and accessible treatment for patients with few available options.

The disease, known as Friedreich ataxia, causes nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord to gradually deteriorate. As the damage progresses, patients lose their ability to coordinate movements, walk, and speak. The condition can also shorten life expectancy, and there is currently no cure. Approximately 200 Australians are living with the disease.

In a new study, scientists found that sulforaphane, a naturally occurring compound in broccoli, can increase levels of frataxin, a protein that is present in insufficient amounts in people with Friedreich ataxia. The researchers also found that the compound can help protect vulnerable nerve cells from damage.

How a Broccoli Compound Could Protect Nerve Cells

Frataxin plays an important role in keeping cells functioning properly, particularly those with high energy demands, such as nerve cells. In Friedreich ataxia, a genetic defect leads to reduced production of this essential protein, contributing to the progressive damage that characterizes the disease.

Sulforaphane appears promising because its potential benefits extend beyond increasing frataxin levels. Research indicates that it can also influence several biological processes involved in disease progression, including cellular stress and inflammation. Addressing multiple sources of damage at once could make the compound a valuable candidate for further investigation.

The findings are particularly encouraging for children with Friedreich ataxia. According to lead researcher Associate Professor Faith Kwa of Swinburne University, children account for a large proportion of those affected, yet no treatments specifically approved for pediatric patients are currently available.

"Friedreich ataxia is a devastating rare genetic disease that progressively steals a child's ability to walk, speak, play, and ultimately survive," she says.

"This novel therapeutic agent can target the underlying cause of the disease, while delivering an affordable and accessible therapy worldwide, improving treatment opportunities for families affected by this life-limiting disease.

"This discovery brings us closer to a future where children with Friedreich ataxia experience a better quality of life, greater independence, and an improved chance of long-term survival."

A Potential Treatment That Could Be More Accessible

One of the most encouraging aspects of sulforaphane is that it is not an entirely unfamiliar substance. The compound already has an established safety record in both children and adults, and purified, biologically active forms are commercially available.

These advantages could make it easier to develop a widely accessible treatment if future clinical trials confirm that sulforaphane is effective against Friedreich ataxia. However, further research is essential before scientists can determine whether the promising findings will translate into meaningful benefits for patients.

Kwa explains that the rarity of Friedreich ataxia creates additional challenges for researchers. Because relatively few people have the disease, public awareness is limited, making it more difficult to attract the funding needed to investigate potential treatments.

Researchers Seek Funding for Clinical Trials

The Swinburne team hopes to secure financial support for clinical trials that would examine whether sulforaphane can deliver the same promising effects in people living with the disease.

"We are hoping to gain funding to conduct clinical trials and further prove the positive impact the broccoli compound could have on those suffering from Friedreich ataxia," she says.

"Sulforaphane already has an established safety record in children and adults, and its pure and bioactive form is commercially available. This means if clinical trials prove successful, its rollout could accelerate the path to patient impact."

For patients and families facing a progressive illness with no cure, even improvements in everyday functioning and independence could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their work will not only advance treatment possibilities but also bring greater attention to a condition that remains largely unknown to the public.

"Even if we can raise awareness of this debilitating condition or improve one person's quality of life, our efforts will have been worth it."

Materials provided by Swinburne University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5662. Opinion: New organ donation rules are unfair to families

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Tucker is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University.

I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.

Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.

Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.

Six months later, our ICU received a letter describing the four lives Hailey had saved. Her kidneys went to two grandparents, each now playing with their grandchildren. Her liver saved a young woman dying of hepatitis who was now snorkeling in a tropical ocean. And her heart was beating inside a young man with a fatal congenital heart condition who was now hiking along the coast.

I’ve never forgotten Hailey or the lives she saved, and I believe deeply in organ donation. But starting Nov. 18, new rules from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network will change how the organ donation process works, allowing organ procurement organizations to approach families about donation before they’ve decided whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.

The goal is to get more viable organs to the more than 100,000 people in the U.S. waiting for life-saving transplants. But I worry this approach blurs the line between the physicians fighting to save a patient’s life and the teams responsible for organ procurement.

That isn’t fair to families, who expect that our sole concern is their loved one’s well-being. Proposing potential organ donation early opens the door to distrust in their ICU care. We should keep that door shut.

In 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services reported 73 cases in which organ donation had been authorized, but not completed, where donors showed “neurological signs incompatible with organ donation.” The New York Times reported that some patients may not have been dead at the time organ procurement was initiated, often in rural or small hospitals.

These findings raised troubling questions about whether the motivation for higher transplant numbers had taken precedence over careful assessment of the neurological condition of potential donors.

The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states, establishes two definitions of death: irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or irreversible loss of function of the entire brain, known as brain death.

To patients’ families, brain death is often harder to grasp than circulatory death. Their loved one appears alive: breathing on a mechanical ventilator, heart still beating steadily on the monitor, skin warm and pink. Yet without mechanical support, if their brain no longer functions, their body will no longer function.

Donation after circulatory death (DCD) involves patients with grave prognoses for whom a decision has been made to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. Many have catastrophic brain injuries, although they do not meet the criteria for brain death. Determining whether a patient is an appropriate candidate for DCD requires a physician’s judgment about the patient’s prognosis, a process that is difficult to standardize.

In contrast, medical standards for determining brain death are uniform and widely practiced in the United States. A diagnosis requires three criteria, as we did for Hailey, rigorously assessed: coma with a known cause, loss of brainstem reflexes, and loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by a strict protocol known as the apnea test.

No one who has been correctly diagnosed with brain death under these criteria has ever recovered. Not one person.

I’m careful to teach our medical students never to say that we “withdraw care” because even when we stop life-sustaining treatment, we continue to care for our patients. Care for the dying is as critical as care for the living.

These decisions require our full attention and the trust of patients’ families, so it’s imperative that a separate organ donation team work alongside us, remaining independent of the physicians treating the patient.

Physicians should be working to increase organ donation while enhancing patient safety.

First, we need to better educate people about what it means to be an organ donor. When someone checks “organ donation” on their driver’s license, they should understand how we define death and what that check mark really means.

Second, we can expand access to neurological expertise in underserved areas, particularly small and rural hospitals that don’t have immediate access to neurologists or neurointensivists. A video consultation with a neurologist or intensive care physician at an academic or comprehensive health care institution can aid in assessing the level of consciousness of patients being considered for DCD, before they’re taken to the operating room for organ recovery.

Another way to increase organ donation is to focus on patients who have been declared brain dead. After brain death, families and health care teams have more time to obtain organs in an orderly fashion, facilitating the best outcome for both donors and recipients.

The ICU clinicians taking care of a patient nearing death are often deep in discussions of the differences (and similarities) between DCD and brain death as they apply to their loved one. The discussions are often confusing and cause conflicted emotions in families facing tragedy.

The new organ procurement organization policy allows donation teams to break into this discussion, often long before family and friends have fully grasped the gravity of the patient’s injury. This interruption can subtly blur the distinction between our caring for the patient and obtaining organs for someone else.

Our first priority must always be the patient before us, and ensuring that the family members making decisions on their behalf understand and trust the care we’re providing.

In the ICU we walk the path of brain death and cardiac death carefully, always remembering that organ donation offers a small piece of biological immortality. Our patients are not yet forever gone.

Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University. Her forthcoming book, “The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments,” will be published in December 2026 by Columbia University Press.

#5661. Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer

Men with very low testosterone levels may face an increased risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease later in life, according to a major international study. The findings suggest that testosterone levels could provide an early clue to future health risks, potentially years or even decades before cancer is diagnosed.

Researchers found that men with low testosterone had an 18 percent higher risk of dying from cancer. However, the relationship was not the same for every type of cancer. Surprisingly, testosterone levels were not associated with prostate cancer risk. Instead, prostate cancer was more closely linked to low levels of two other hormones, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and luteinizing hormone.

The research comes from the Androgens In Men Study (AIMS), an international collaboration led by Professor Bu Yeap at The University of Western Australia. The project investigates how different sex hormones relate to cancer risk and other health outcomes in men.

Study Tracks Testosterone and Cancer Risk in 26,000 Men

Published in the journal Lancet Healthy Longevity, the study examined data from more than 26,000 men participating in 11 long-running studies across Australia, the United States, and Europe.

Researchers analyzed hormone concentrations in blood samples collected earlier in the men's lives. They then compared those measurements with cancer diagnoses and deaths recorded over the following decades, allowing them to investigate whether hormone levels were associated with future cancer outcomes.

The analysis included testosterone, dihydrotestosterone (DHT), SHBG, and luteinizing hormone. Luteinizing hormone is produced by the pituitary gland and signals the testes to produce testosterone.

"We wanted to know whether the concentration of these hormones in the blood was related to the risk of men being diagnosed with, or dying from, cancer into the future," Professor Yeap said.

"What we saw was that if a man had low testosterone levels - in the lowest one-fifth compared to the highest one-fifth of the range - their subsequent risk of dying from cancer was higher, even after allowing for age and other health-related factors."

Cancer Risk Increased Below a Key Testosterone Level

The researchers identified a testosterone concentration below which cancer risk began to rise. According to Professor Yeap, testosterone levels in healthy younger men typically range from 10 to 30 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L), although concentrations generally decrease with age.

Testosterone levels can also be influenced by factors that people may be able to change, including body mass index and physical activity. Certain medical conditions, such as diabetes, can affect testosterone concentrations as well.

"We saw that when baseline testosterone was below 8.6 nmol/L, subsequent cancer risk started increasing," Professor Yeap said.

"This suggests low testosterone is an important biomarker, so it's possible that looking at testosterone levels could help us identify men who might do poorly if they get cancer down the track."

These findings raise the possibility that testosterone measurements could help doctors recognize men who may face greater health risks in the future. However, the results show an association and do not establish that low testosterone itself causes cancer.

A Surprising Finding About Prostate Cancer

Because testosterone plays an important role in male reproductive health, researchers also investigated whether naturally occurring testosterone levels influenced the likelihood of developing prostate cancer.

The question has particular medical significance because lowering testosterone is an established treatment for prostate cancer. However, the new analysis found no evidence that a man's natural testosterone concentration was associated with his risk of developing the disease.

"Since reducing testosterone levels is a treatment for prostate cancer there's always been a question of whether the amount of testosterone your own body makes relates to your risk of prostate cancer but based on our findings there's no evidence they are related," Professor Yeap said.

"We did find, however, that men with low levels of SHBG and luteinizing hormone were at higher risk of prostate cancer."

The results highlight an important distinction between testosterone and other hormones involved in male reproductive function. Although low testosterone was associated with higher overall cancer risk and mortality, prostate cancer showed a different pattern of hormonal associations.

Why Low Testosterone Does Not Mean Men Need Supplements

Despite the connection between low testosterone and cancer outcomes, Professor Yeap emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation to take testosterone supplements to prevent cancer.

"While we've shown low levels are associated with increased risk, we haven't got any evidence yet that actually giving men testosterone will reduce that risk," he said.

Instead, unexpectedly low testosterone could be a reason to investigate a person's overall health. A medical evaluation may uncover underlying conditions or risk factors that require attention, even when there is no evidence of a problem affecting the testes.

"What we would say to men is if they are found for whatever reason to be low in testosterone, it's important to go to the doctor for a full checkup. It may not show any sign of testicular disease, but it might show other health issues or risk factors they need to address.

"It could be a wake-up call and encouragement for men to engage in more healthy lifestyle behaviors, and to get regular, holistic checkups to stay on top of their health."

Materials provided by University of Western Australia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5659. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

Social media platforms allow you to connect directly with your target audience too. You can answer queries and concerns in your DMs and show the human side of your brand.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

Optimize your videos for search engines by including keywords and phrases in your video titles and descriptions. Doing so increases your rankings on SERPs and puts your brand in front of as many people as possible.

#5657. Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect

A new study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations.

The research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience, found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form new connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons.

Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug.

The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions.

The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress.

"I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.

Why Scientists Are Taking a New Look at Psychedelics

Scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood.

Early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances.

In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function.

Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons.

This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions.

In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs."

Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed.

As regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer.

To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy.

This technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment.

Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate.

Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain.

Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines.

But the drug did more than encourage new connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace.

Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections.

After psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons.

Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood.

For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin.

"Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab.

"These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain."

Psilocybin Affects Healthy and Stressed Brains Differently

One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress.

In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level.

This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance.

The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress.

To investigate this, they used an unpredictable mild stress model, which exposes animals to varying low-intensity stressors and produces changes that resemble certain features of human depression.

Prolonged stress is known to interfere with neural communication and can cause substantial losses of synaptic connections. Over time, these changes can weaken the circuits involved in important brain functions.

When the stressed mice received psilocybin, the researchers observed an especially strong increase in the formation of new dendritic spines.

At the same time, psilocybin prevented the unusually high rate of connection loss associated with chronic stress.

Together, these effects suggest that psilocybin may do more than temporarily increase the number of connections in the brain. Under stressful conditions, it may also help preserve existing connections and restore circuitry that has been disrupted.

"These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain's underlying condition," Zuo added.

"This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders."

Could Psilocybin Rewire the Brain Without Hallucinations?

Perhaps the most significant implication of the research concerns a longstanding question in psychedelic medicine: Are hallucinations and altered states of consciousness necessary for the brain changes that might contribute to therapeutic benefits?

To explore this possibility, the scientists examined the role of serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs), which are proteins on the surfaces of cells that respond to chemical signals. These receptors are central to the effects of psilocybin and other classic psychedelics.

The researchers focused on a group of nerve cells called Layer 5 pyramidal neurons. These cells are located in the cerebral cortex, the outer region of the brain involved in complex functions such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

Layer 5 pyramidal neurons serve as important communication pathways that send information from the cortex to other brain regions. They also contain high levels of serotonin 2A receptors, making them especially relevant to understanding psilocybin's effects.

Using genetically modified mice, the team selectively changed whether these neurons possessed the receptors.

The results revealed a striking separation between changes in brain connections and a behavior associated with psychedelic activity.

When the researchers restored serotonin 2A receptors only in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin was still able to stimulate the development of new synapses and help stabilize them.

Surprisingly, these mice did not display the characteristic head twitch response that researchers commonly use as an indicator of psychedelic activity in rodents.

The scientists then performed the opposite experiment.

When they removed serotonin 2A receptors specifically from Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin lost its ability to stimulate the same structural growth of synapses.

However, the mice still exhibited the head twitch response.

These contrasting results demonstrate that serotonin 2A receptor signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for the structural brain changes observed in the experiments, while those same receptors are not required for the psychedelic-associated behavioral response.

In other words, the cellular pathway responsible for psilocybin's brain rewiring can be separated from the pathway responsible for this particular behavioral marker of psychedelic activity.

Because mice cannot describe subjective experiences, the head twitch response does not directly establish whether an animal is experiencing hallucinations. Nevertheless, the findings provide important evidence that these two effects involve distinct cellular mechanisms.

A Potential Path Toward Psychedelic Treatments Without the Trip

The discovery could have major implications for the development of future psychiatric medications.

If researchers can identify compounds that activate the brain's ability to rebuild and reorganize neural connections without triggering psychedelic effects, it may become possible to create treatments that preserve some of psilocybin's therapeutic potential while avoiding the need for patients to undergo intense altered states of consciousness.

Such medications could be easier to administer and might require less intensive clinical supervision than conventional psychedelic-assisted therapies.

"By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs," Zuo said.

"Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects -- making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population."

Although the results are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the same cellular mechanisms operate in humans and whether separating brain rewiring from psychedelic effects can produce effective treatments for depression, PTSD, or other psychiatric disorders.

For now, the findings provide a more detailed picture of how psilocybin changes the brain and reveal a potential strategy for harnessing its effects on neural connections without relying on the psychedelic experience itself.

The study's other UC Santa Cruz coauthors include molecular and cell biologists Jacob Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, and Ju Lu, alongside Zuo.

Funding came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging. The psilocybin used in the experiments was supplied through the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Drug Supply Program.

Materials provided by University of California - Santa Cruz. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5656. 3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle

The healthcare revenue cycle depends on teams investigating denied claims, checking payer rules and deciding which problems need a human’s attention. AI agents could take on some of that work, but the harder question is how to fit them into the way health systems operate.

For Mount Sinai Health System Inc., that starts with clear workflows and accountability when automation encounters an exception, according to Salonia Brown, system vice president of revenue cycle at Mount Sinai. Without those foundations, adding AI could make existing problems harder to manage.

“If you don’t have your workflows down pat, if you don’t have operational owners, when something kicks out, when you use AI, if there’s no ownership over that or accountability, then what you’re in essence doing is kind of digitizing dysfunction,” Brown said in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s very simple and easy to inject AI, but to do it the right way, making sure there’s governance [and] that the economics make sense? That takes a little bit of time.”

Brown and Akash Magoon, co-founder and chief executive officer of Adonis Technology Inc., along with other industry experts, spoke with theCUBE’s host Gemma Allen for the Adonis Reimagining Claim to Cash interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents can handle claims work, how health systems govern exceptions and where human judgment remains essential. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are three insights from this exclusive interview series:

Adonis is building agents to investigate denied claims and reduce the manual work involved in pursuing payment, according to Magoon. The company uses voice AI to call insurers for claims information and makes tens of thousands of those calls each week on behalf of its partners.

At Mount Sinai, Brown’s team helps determine which tasks can be automated and which require critical judgment. Employees need to trust the technology and know who is responsible when an exception arises, he noted. The goal is to free staff from repetitive administrative work so they can focus on more complex cases.

Adonis distinguishes between frequent, repetitive tasks suited to automation and complex work that calls for better information and decisions, according to David Unger, managing director of health system sales at Adonis. For a high-value appeal, that can mean helping a team decide whether to pursue it and what evidence may improve its chances.

At Rush University System for Health, frontline employees help identify time-consuming steps that add little value, according to Blake Evans, system vice president of revenue cycle at Rush. Their firsthand knowledge helps the company decide where to automate and has made staff advocates for further changes.

Adonis aims to identify revenue-cycle issues as they emerge and recommend a response, according to Doug Pickett, chief revenue officer of Adonis. An issue might call for automation, or it might reveal an upstream coding or provider-credentialing problem that a health system needs to fix before it grows.

Clinicians and operating teams are increasingly asking for AI tools that could reduce administrative burdens, according to Sap Sinha, chief executive officer of Panoramic Health. Yet rules governing billing, documentation and interactions with insurers have not kept pace with the technology. How those rules evolve could shape whether and how providers and insurers can use AI agents to interact over claims.

Check out the full discussion on theCUBE.

#5655. MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.
